cau_hoi: In the food chain "grass → rabbit → fox", which organism is the producer?
giai_thich: Producers, like green plants and algae, create organic matter through photosynthesis and are the first link in most food chains. The rabbit, which eats grass, is a primary consumer, while the fox, which eats the rabbit, is a secondary consumer. Energy from the Sun is gradually transferred through each link. Without producers, the entire food chain would collapse.

cau_hoi: Which dinosaur is famous for being a large predator with huge teeth and very short arms?
giai_thich: Tyrannosaurus rex was about 12 – 13 meters long, weighed around 8 – 9 tons, and lived at the end of the Cretaceous period in North America, about 68 – 66 million years ago. Its bite force was likely the strongest of any land animal that ever lived. Its short arms were only about 1 meter long but muscular. The name means "tyrant lizard king."

cau_hoi: Which of the following actions helps protect the environment?
giai_thich: Sorting waste helps recycle paper, plastic, and metal into new products, saving resources and energy. Organic waste can be composted into fertilizer. Burning plastic produces toxic gases, while littering in rivers ultimately leads to the ocean, harming turtles, fish, and seabirds. Everyone can contribute by using cloth bags and personal water bottles instead of single-use plastic.

cau_hoi: Which bird became extinct in the 17th century on the island of Mauritius, becoming a symbol of extinction?
giai_thich: The dodo was a giant flightless pigeon, about 1 meter tall. Living on an island without predators, they did not fear humans. After the Dutch arrived on the island in 1598, dodos were hunted, and rats, pigs, and monkeys brought by humans ate their eggs. The last recorded dodo was around 1662. The English phrase "dead as a dodo" means completely extinct.

cau_hoi: Who is the scientist famous for the theory of evolution by natural selection, presented in the book "On the Origin of Species" (1859)?
giai_thich: Charles Darwin traveled around the world on the Beagle (1831 – 1836), observing fossils, flora, and fauna in South America and the Galápagos Islands. He spent over 20 years gathering evidence before publishing his book. The main idea: individuals with traits suited to their environment survive and reproduce more, gradually leading to species change.

cau_hoi: Why are many wild animals like tigers, elephants, and rhinos threatened?
C: Loss of habitat and illegal hunting
D: Because the weather is too nice
giai_thich: Forests are being cleared for agriculture and construction, causing animals to lose their habitats and food sources. Poaching for ivory, rhino horns, and tiger skins also drives many species to the brink of extinction. Currently, the number of wild tigers in the world is only about 5,000 – 6,000. Not buying or using products from wild animals is a way everyone can help protect them.

cau_hoi: In an ecosystem, which organisms decompose the remains of plants and animals into nutrients returned to the soil?
giai_thich: Bacteria, fungi, earthworms, and many insect species decompose dead bodies and fallen leaves, turning them into minerals that plants absorb. Without decomposers, the Earth would be flooded with dead bodies and dry leaves, and nutrients would be "locked" away. That is why they are referred to as nature's "clean-up crew."

cau_hoi: When did dinosaurs (excluding birds) go extinct?
giai_thich: About 66 million years ago, an asteroid about 10 km wide struck the Earth in what is now the Yucatán Peninsula (Mexico). Dust and smoke blocked sunlight, killing plants and causing a sudden climate change, leading to the extinction of about 75% of species, including non-flying dinosaurs. Humans only appeared about 300,000 years ago, so they never lived alongside dinosaurs.

cau_hoi: Which animal is considered by scientists today to be a living descendant of dinosaurs?
giai_thich: Birds evolved from a group of small feathered theropod dinosaurs, relatives of the Velociraptor. Many feathered dinosaur fossils have been found in China since the 1990s. Therefore, in a scientific sense, chickens and sparrows are indeed "living dinosaurs." Crocodiles are the closest living relatives of dinosaurs and birds, but they are not dinosaurs.

cau_hoi: Which layer of the atmosphere protects the Earth from harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun?
giai_thich: The ozone layer is located at an altitude of about 15 – 35 km, absorbing most harmful ultraviolet rays. Without it, life on land would struggle to survive. CFCs, once used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays, have depleted the ozone layer, but thanks to the Montreal Protocol in 1987 banning these substances, the ozone layer is gradually recovering. This is a significant success of international environmental cooperation.

cau_hoi: The phenomenon of global warming is primarily caused by the release of which gas by humans?
D: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) and other greenhouse gases
giai_thich: When burning coal, oil, and gas to produce electricity, drive vehicles, and run factories, humans release large amounts of CO₂. Greenhouse gases trap heat like a blanket around the Earth. The concentration of CO₂ has increased from about 280 parts per million before the Industrial Revolution to over 420 parts per million today. The consequences include melting ice, rising sea levels, and more extreme weather.

cau_hoi: When a species has no living individuals left on Earth, what do we say has happened to that species?
giai_thich: Scientists estimate that over 99% of species that have ever lived on Earth are now extinct. Extinction is a natural part of the history of life, but today the rate of extinction is happening tens to hundreds of times faster than the natural rate due to human activities. Once a species is extinct, it cannot return. June 5th each year is World Environment Day.

cau_hoi: What is the relationship called when both bees and flowers benefit?
giai_thich: Bees collect nectar and pollen for food, while flowers benefit from bees helping with pollination to produce fruit. Other examples include clownfish and sea anemones, bacteria in the roots of leguminous plants, and bacteria in the human gut. In parasitic relationships, like lice on hair, one party benefits while the other is harmed. These relationships help ecosystems stay interconnected.

cau_hoi: How does a food web differ from a food chain?
A: It has only one single path
D: It consists of many interwoven food chains because each species eats and is eaten by many species
giai_thich: In nature, few species eat only one type of food. For example, mice eat seeds and insects, and are then eaten by snakes, owls, and foxes. Food chains connect to form complex food webs. The more diverse the web, the more stable the ecosystem: if one species declines, others can find alternative food sources.

cau_hoi: Why is the forest called the "green lungs" of the Earth?
A: Trees absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen
B: Because forests have a lot of water
giai_thich: Trees in forests absorb CO₂ during photosynthesis and store carbon in their trunks, roots, and soil. Forests also retain water, prevent erosion, regulate climate, and are home to over 80% of terrestrial species. Vietnam has a forest cover of about 42%. Planting trees and protecting forests helps reduce climate change and flooding.

cau_hoi: Chameleons, stick insects, and caterpillars have colors and shapes that resemble their surroundings. What does this characteristic help them do?
B: To camouflage to avoid predators or ambush prey
giai_thich: Camouflage is one of the most visible examples of natural selection: individuals that are harder to detect survive and reproduce more. Stick insects look like dry twigs, and leaf butterflies fold their wings to resemble leaves with veins. Polar bears are white like snow, while tigers have stripes like shadows of grass and trees.

cau_hoi: What is a fossil?
D: The trace or remains of an ancient organism preserved in rock
giai_thich: When an organism dies and is quickly buried in mud or sand, hard parts like bones, shells, and teeth can gradually be replaced by minerals and turn into rock over millions of years. Footprints, eggs, feces, and even skin impressions can also become fossils. Fossils are important evidence that life has changed over time.

cau_hoi: During which period did the woolly mammoth live?
A: The Ice Age, until about 4,000 years ago
B: Only a few hundred years ago
C: At the same time as dinosaurs
giai_thich: Woolly mammoths had thick fur and a layer of fat for cold protection, living in the icy grasslands of Europe, Asia, and North America. Most disappeared about 10,000 years ago, but a small population lived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago, when the Egyptians had already built the pyramids. Many woolly mammoth remains have been found almost perfectly preserved in Siberian permafrost.

cau_hoi: In an ecosystem, what percentage of energy is typically transferred from one trophic level to the next?
giai_thich: Most energy at each level is lost through respiration, heat, waste, and parts that are not consumed. Therefore, in an ecosystem, a lot of grass is needed to feed a few herbivores, and many herbivores are needed to sustain one tiger. This is why food chains rarely exceed 4-5 links, and large predators are always fewer in number.

cau_hoi: Which bird did Charles Darwin observe on the Galápagos Islands that had different beaks suited to the food on each island?
giai_thich: The finch species on the Galápagos likely evolved from a common ancestor that flew from South America. The seed-eating species have strong, large beaks, while insect-eating species have sharp, slender beaks, and some even use cactus spines to extract insects. Since 1973, scientists Peter and Rosemary Grant have been monitoring finches on Daphne Major Island and have witnessed changes in beak shape after just a few years of drought.

cau_hoi: What is the first national park of Vietnam, established in 1962?
giai_thich: Cúc Phương National Park is located between the three provinces of Ninh Bình, Hòa Bình, and old Thanh Hóa, in a limestone mountainous area with primary forests. Here, there are thousand-year-old trees, caves with traces of prehistoric people, and a center for rescuing endangered primates. Cúc Phương is famous for its butterfly season around April to May, when millions of butterflies fill the forest paths.

cau_hoi: What does the term "biodiversity" refer to?
B: The richness of species, genes, and ecosystems
C: The number of people on Earth
giai_thich: Biodiversity includes three levels: genetic diversity within a species, species diversity, and ecosystem diversity such as forests, seas, and wetlands. Scientists have described about 2 million species, but there may be millions more yet to be discovered. Vietnam is one of about 16 countries with the highest biodiversity in the world.

cau_hoi: Which species is considered a "keystone species" in the Pacific coastal kelp forest ecosystem?
giai_thich: Sea otters eat sea urchins. When otters were hunted to near extinction for their fur, sea urchins exploded in population, stripping kelp forests and turning them into "urchin deserts." When otters were protected and returned, kelp forests recovered, bringing back fish and many other species. A keystone species has a disproportionately large impact on its ecosystem relative to its abundance.

cau_hoi: How can butterflies, migratory birds, and trees be affected by climate warming?
C: Change in flowering time, migration, and shift their habitats higher or towards the poles
giai_thich: Many studies show that plants are flowering earlier, birds are migrating earlier, and many species are shifting their habitats an average of about 17 km towards the poles each decade. If the timing of flowering and pollinating insects no longer coincide, both are harmed. Species living at mountain tops or polar regions have nowhere left to "run".

cau_hoi: According to Darwin, what is the main mechanism leading to the evolution of species?
giai_thich: Natural selection consists of three ideas: individuals in a species vary slightly; some differences are heritable; and individuals with traits suited to the environment survive and leave more offspring. Over many generations, beneficial traits become common. Animals cannot "want" to change; changes occur in populations over long periods.

cau_hoi: Which scientist independently conceived the theory of natural selection at the same time as Darwin while studying in the Malay Archipelago?
giai_thich: In 1858, while suffering from malaria in the Maluku Islands (Indonesia), Wallace wrote to Darwin presenting ideas very similar to Darwin's. Darwin was very surprised, and that same year, the ideas of both were presented together at the Linnean Society in London. Wallace also discovered "Wallace's line," a boundary dividing Asian and Australian animals.

cau_hoi: The "peppered moth" species in England during the Industrial Revolution is a classic example of what?
A: Natural selection: dark moths became more common as tree trunks were blackened by soot
giai_thich: Previously, most moths were light-colored, blending in with the lichen on tree trunks. When factory smoke blackened tree trunks, light-colored moths were more easily spotted by birds, while dark moths survived more. By the late 19th century, most moths in Manchester were dark. When the air became clean again after 1956, light-colored moths regained dominance.

cau_hoi: What wild animal was domesticated to create the domestic dog?
giai_thich: DNA studies show that dogs originated from an ancient population of wolves, domesticated about 15,000 years ago or earlier, making them the first domesticated animal. Through artificial selection, humans have created hundreds of different dog breeds, from the 2 kg Chihuahua to the over 100 kg English Mastiff, but they all remain the same species.

cau_hoi: Which international convention recognizes coastal areas with mangrove forests and mudflats that help migratory birds rest, such as Xuân Thủy National Park (old Nam Định)?
giai_thich: Xuân Thủy is the first Ramsar site in Vietnam and Southeast Asia, recognized in 1989. It is a stopover for many rare migratory bird species such as spoon-billed storks and black-faced spoonbills. The Ramsar Convention, signed in 1971 in Ramsar (Iran), protects wetlands such as swamps, river mouths, and mangrove forests. February 2nd each year is World Wetlands Day.

cau_hoi: What is the IUCN Red List used for?
B: Assessing and listing the extinction risk levels of species
giai_thich: The Red List of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies species into categories such as least concern, near threatened, vulnerable, endangered, critically endangered, extinct in the wild, and extinct. Currently, over 160,000 species have been assessed, of which more than 45,000 are threatened. Vietnam also has its own Red List.

cau_hoi: The phenomenon where different species, not closely related, have similar shapes due to living in similar environments is called what?
giai_thich: Sharks (fish), dolphins (mammals), and the extinct marine reptile ichthyosaur all have streamlined bodies, dorsal fins, and strong tails because that is the best shape for swimming fast. Bird wings, bat wings, and insect wings have also evolved independently. These examples show that natural selection often finds similar 'solutions' to the same problem.

cau_hoi: The French scientist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck once explained why giraffes have long necks in a way that is now considered incorrect. What was his explanation?
A: Because giraffes stretch their necks to eat high leaves, their necks lengthen and they pass this trait to their offspring
B: Because giraffes eat a lot of grass
giai_thich: Lamarck (early 19th century) believed that traits acquired through use during life could be inherited. However, a weightlifter with large muscles does not give birth to muscular offspring. According to Darwin, giraffes with slightly longer necks could eat more leaves and survive better. Although incorrect, Lamarck made significant contributions as one of the first to propose that species change over time.

cau_hoi: What are the remnants in the body that no longer have significant functions, such as the small pelvis in whales, called?
giai_thich: Some whale species have small pelvic bones deep in their bodies, remnants of ancestors that once had hind legs on land. Pythons have small 'spurs' as remnants of hind limbs. In humans, the coccyx and the auricular muscles are examples. Vestigial organs provide evidence that species have common ancestors and have changed over time.

cau_hoi: What do we call species that are introduced by humans to a new environment, proliferate rapidly, and harm native species?
giai_thich: In a new environment, invasive species often lack natural predators, allowing them to explode in population. In Vietnam, the golden apple snail was introduced in the 1980s for food but escaped into rice fields, eating young rice and causing significant damage. The glass catfish, the mai duong plant, and water hyacinth are also invasive species in our country. Preventing the release of foreign species into the wild is an important preventive measure.

cau_hoi: What role do coral reefs play in the ocean, even though they occupy less than 1% of the ocean floor?
B: They are home to about a quarter of all marine species
giai_thich: Coral reefs are likened to the 'tropical rainforests of the ocean.' They are breeding, feeding, and sheltering grounds for thousands of species of fish, shrimp, crabs, and turtles. Coral reefs also break waves, protect coastlines, and provide tourism and fishery benefits. In Vietnam, the waters of Nha Trang, Con Dao, Phu Quoc, and Cu Lao Cham have many beautiful coral reefs that need protection.

cau_hoi: What is the phenomenon called when algae overgrow in ponds due to nutrient-rich wastewater, causing fish to die from lack of oxygen?
giai_thich: Fertilizers and domestic wastewater containing high levels of nitrogen and phosphorus flow into ponds, causing algae to bloom densely. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them and consume all the oxygen in the water, causing fish and other organisms to suffocate. At the mouth of the Mississippi River (USA), a 'dead zone' lacking oxygen forms every summer, covering thousands of square kilometers. Treating wastewater and applying fertilizers appropriately helps mitigate this phenomenon.

cau_hoi: In 1962, Rachel Carson's book 'Silent Spring' warned about the harmful effects of which substance, contributing to the start of the environmental protection movement?
giai_thich: Carson pointed out that DDT accumulates in the food chain, causing the eggshells of predatory birds like the bald eagle and the osprey to become thin and break during incubation. The title of the book evokes a spring without the sound of birds singing. In 1972, the US banned the use of DDT in agriculture, and the population of bald eagles, the national symbol of the USA, has rebounded strongly.

cau_hoi: What is the phenomenon called when toxins like mercury and DDT have increasingly higher concentrations as they move up the food chain?
giai_thich: Toxins that are difficult to break down accumulate in the fatty tissues of organisms. Plankton absorb small amounts, small fish eat many plankton, and large fish eat many small fish, so concentrations increase thousands to millions of times at the top of the food chain. Therefore, large predatory fish that live long, like swordfish and sharks, can contain high levels of mercury, and pregnant women are advised to limit their consumption of these fish.

cau_hoi: In 1995, what surprising change occurred after wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park (USA)?
B: The deer population decreased and changed behavior, allowing riverside trees to regrow, leading to beavers and birds returning
giai_thich: After wolves were hunted to extinction in the 1920s, the elk population surged and stripped willow and young aspen trees along the riverbanks. When 31 wolves were reintroduced in 1995-1996, elk avoided open areas, allowing trees to regrow, beavers to have wood to build dams, and fish and birds to have more habitats. This cascading effect through multiple levels is called 'trophic cascade,' although the extent of its impact is still debated by scientists.

cau_hoi: The passenger pigeon in North America once had a massive population. What happened to them?
C: They were hunted to extinction; the last one died in 1914
giai_thich: In the 19th century, there were perhaps 3 to 5 billion passenger pigeons, with flocks so large they could darken the sky for hours. They were hunted en masse for meat, coupled with deforestation. The last one, named Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. This serves as a lesson that even species with massive populations can go extinct very quickly.

cau_hoi: The Tasmanian tiger (thylacine), the largest modern carnivorous marsupial, is believed to have gone extinct when?
A: At the same time as the dinosaurs
D: The last one died in Hobart Zoo in 1936
giai_thich: The Tasmanian tiger resembled a dog with stripes on its back, but it was a marsupial, more closely related to kangaroos than to dogs, a great example of convergent evolution. They were hunted because they were thought to kill sheep, and the government even offered rewards for each one killed. The last one, later named Benjamin, died on September 7, 1936, due to being left outside in the cold. September 7 is now Australia’s Threatened Species Day.

cau_hoi: Scientists believe that Earth has experienced how many major mass extinctions in the last 500 million years?
giai_thich: The five major mass extinctions occurred at the end of the Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, and Cretaceous periods (which led to the extinction of the dinosaurs). Each time, a large portion of species disappeared in a short geological timeframe. Many scientists warn that the current rate of species loss due to humans may be leading to a sixth mass extinction.

cau_hoi: Which mass extinction is considered the worst in Earth's history, causing about 90% of marine species to disappear?
C: End of the Permian period, about 252 million years ago
giai_thich: This event is known as the "Great Dying." The main cause was likely massive volcanic eruptions in Siberia that lasted for hundreds of thousands of years, releasing huge amounts of CO₂, causing the Earth to heat up significantly, oceans to acidify, and oxygen levels to drop. After the event, life took about 10 million years to recover, and dinosaurs appeared in that new world.

cau_hoi: The Archaeopteryx fossil, discovered in Germany in 1861, is famous for showing what?
B: A transitional creature with feathers, bird-like wings, but also teeth and a bony tail like a dinosaur
giai_thich: Archaeopteryx lived about 150 million years ago, roughly the size of a crow. It was found just two years after Darwin published "On the Origin of Species," becoming a famous piece of evidence supporting the theory of evolution. The fossil is beautifully preserved in fine-grained limestone at Solnhofen, retaining even feather impressions. Today, it is known that many other dinosaurs also had feathers.

cau_hoi: The Tiktaalik fossil, published in 2006, is considered a transitional link between which groups of animals?
giai_thich: Tiktaalik lived about 375 million years ago, had scales and fins like fish, but also had a neck, a flat head like a crocodile, lungs, and front fins containing wrist-like bones, helping support its body in shallow waters. Scientists predicted it should be found in rocks of that age, and indeed it was found on Ellesmere Island (Canada). The name Tiktaalik in Inuktitut means a large freshwater fish.

cau_hoi: What was the "Cambrian Explosion" event around 538 – 520 million years ago?
A: The rapid appearance of most major animal phyla in the fossil record
giai_thich: In about 20 – 25 million years, a short time in geological terms, fossils show the emergence of animals with eyes, jointed legs, hard shells, and even the ancestors of vertebrates. Scientists believe that increased oxygen levels, the emergence of predators, and genetic changes drove this explosion. Trilobites are one of the symbols of the Cambrian period.

cau_hoi: When did trilobites, one of the most famous fossil groups, go extinct?
A: At the same time as the dinosaurs
C: At the end of the Permian period, about 252 million years ago
giai_thich: Trilobites were marine arthropods that lived for about 270 million years with over 20,000 known species. Their eyes are among the oldest, with lenses made of calcite crystals. They could roll up like a pill bug when threatened. The mass extinction at the end of the Permian wiped out the last trilobite species.

cau_hoi: How can the unique ecosystem in the Son Doong cave system exist?
B: Thanks to sinkholes in the cave ceiling allowing light in, with a forest growing inside the cave
giai_thich: Son Doong Cave in Phong Nha – Ke Bang National Park is one of the largest caves in the world, thoroughly surveyed in 2009. Two large sinkholes in the cave ceiling allow light and rain to enter, creating a forest with trees several dozen meters tall, insects, birds, and monkeys living inside. The cave also contains large cave pearls the size of baseballs and an underground river.

cau_hoi: Why do animal species living on small islands often have unusual sizes, such as dwarf elephants or giant lizards?
A: Due to limited food sources and fewer predators, natural selection causes large species to shrink and small species to grow
B: Because the islands are too hot
giai_thich: This phenomenon is called the "island rule." On islands, food is scarce, so large species like elephants and hippos tend to shrink, for example, dwarf elephants that once lived on the island of Sicily were only about 1 meter tall. Conversely, in the absence of predators, smaller species like mice, lizards, and birds can grow larger, such as the Komodo dragon in Indonesia or the dodo bird in Mauritius.

cau_hoi: Why are humans classified as primates?
B: They share many characteristics with monkeys and apes, such as grasping hands, forward-facing eyes, and large brains
giai_thich: The primate order includes lemurs, monkeys, apes, and humans. Common features include hands with opposable thumbs for grasping, flat nails instead of claws, two eyes facing forward for depth perception, and large brains relative to body size. The closest living relatives of humans are chimpanzees and bonobos, who share a common ancestor with humans about 6 – 7 million years ago.

cau_hoi: According to scientists, in which continent did modern humans (Homo sapiens) first appear?
giai_thich: The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, about 300,000 years old, were found in Jebel Irhoud (Morocco). Genetic evidence shows that all people today have ancestors in Africa. About 50,000 – 70,000 years ago, a group of modern humans left Africa and gradually spread across the world. Those who reached Southeast Asia, possibly including Vietnam, did so relatively early on this journey.

cau_hoi: Which creature lives at the top of the ocean food chain, eating even great white sharks?
giai_thich: Orcas are the top predators of the ocean, with no natural enemies. In South Africa, a pair of orcas named Port and Starboard have hunted many great white sharks, only eating their oil-rich livers, causing great whites to flee from these waters. Top predators are crucial for keeping the populations of species below them in balance.

cau_hoi: What is the term for humans selectively breeding plants and animals over generations?
giai_thich: From a wild cabbage species, humans have selected varieties to create cabbage (selecting leaf buds), cauliflower (selecting flower clusters), kale (selecting leaves), kohlrabi (selecting stems), Brussels sprouts (selecting buds), and broccoli. All are the same species, Brassica oleracea. Darwin used the example of artificial selection, particularly with fancy pigeons, to explain natural selection.

cau_hoi: What is the main cause of the increasing acidity of the oceans (ocean acidification)?
C: The ocean absorbs large amounts of CO₂ from the atmosphere
giai_thich: The ocean absorbs about a quarter of the CO₂ emitted by humans. CO₂ dissolves to form carbonic acid, causing the pH of seawater to drop from about 8.2 to 8.1 since pre-industrial times, equivalent to an increase in acidity of about 30%. More acidic seawater makes it difficult for corals, clams, and many planktonic organisms to form calcium carbonate shells.

cau_hoi: Why do scientists consider mangrove trees as a "green shield" during tsunamis and storms?
A: Because the trees calm the sea immediately
B: Because the trees create stone walls
C: Because the trees absorb all the seawater
D: The dense root system reduces wave strength and holds the coastal soil
giai_thich: After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, studies showed that villages behind mangrove forests suffered less damage. A strip of mangrove forest about 100 meters wide can significantly reduce wave height. Mangroves also store carbon many times more than terrestrial forests of the same area, hence they are called "blue carbon."

cau_hoi: Why should you not release fish or turtles of unknown origin into rivers and lakes when "liberating" them?
A: Because the river water is too clean
B: They may be invasive species that harm native species and spread diseases
D: Because they will grow as large as whales
giai_thich: Many species released, such as red-eared sliders, glass catfish, and white bass, are of foreign origin and can compete for food, eat the eggs of native fish, and carry diseases. The red-eared slider is on the list of the 100 most dangerous invasive species in the world. Additionally, many animals caught from the wild are sold for release and die after being set free. Be sure to research or ask rescue centers before releasing.

cau_hoi: What is the biggest cause of biodiversity loss in the world today?
C: Habitat loss and degradation due to land conversion for agriculture and urbanization
giai_thich: According to the 2019 IPBES global assessment report, the top cause is land and sea use change, followed by overexploitation (fishing, hunting), climate change, pollution, and invasive alien species. About 1 million species of plants and animals are at risk of extinction. Protecting and restoring forests and wetlands is the most effective way to retain biodiversity.

cau_hoi: Some non-toxic butterfly species mimic the colors of toxic butterflies to avoid being eaten by birds. What is this phenomenon called?
giai_thich: In 1862, naturalist Henry Walter Bates observed in the Amazon rainforest that many harmless butterfly species looked exactly like bitter-tasting butterflies that birds avoid eating. The mimics are protected "secondarily." Another example: some fly species with yellow and black stripes resemble bees, or harmless milk snakes have color bands similar to those of venomous coral snakes.

cau_hoi: What is the phenomenon called when two toxic species evolve to have similar warning shapes and colors, helping predators learn faster?
giai_thich: German naturalist Fritz Müller explained in 1878: if two toxic species look alike, birds only need to try one to learn the lesson for both species, so both benefit. Examples include many species of wasps and hornets with yellow and black stripes, or Heliconius butterflies that are toxic in South America. Monarch butterflies and viceroy butterflies are also considered an example.

cau_hoi: In peafowl, the male has a huge, colorful tail despite being easily spotted by predators. Which theory did Darwin explain this with?
B: Sexual selection: females prefer to choose males with beautiful tails
giai_thich: Darwin once wrote that seeing peacock feathers made him "sick," as it seemed contrary to natural selection. He explained it through sexual selection: males with beautiful tails are chosen more by females, leaving more offspring, even if they die earlier. Beautiful plumage may be a sign that the male is healthy and has fewer parasites.

cau_hoi: In Lake Victoria (Africa), hundreds of cichlid species have evolved from just a few ancestors in about 15,000 years. What is the phenomenon called when one ancestor splits into many species adapted to different lifestyles?
giai_thich: Cichlid species in Lake Victoria have different jaws and teeth: some eat algae on rocks, some crush snails, some eat the scales of other fish, and even some eat the eggs of other fish. The lake nearly dried up about 15,000 years ago, so diversification occurred very rapidly. Unfortunately, when Nile perch were introduced to the lake in the 1950s, hundreds of cichlid species disappeared.

cau_hoi: What is typically the first organism to inhabit a new volcanic island or a bare rock?
giai_thich: Lichens are a symbiosis between fungi and algae, capable of attaching to bare rocks, secreting acid that gradually breaks down the rock into soil. Moss follows, then grasses, shrubs, and finally forests. This gradual change in community structure over time is called ecological succession. After the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883 wiped out all life, the island had forests again in just about 50 years.

cau_hoi: What is the maximum number of individuals of a species that the environment can sustainably support called?
giai_thich: When a new population arrives in an area with abundant food, the number increases rapidly. However, as it approaches carrying capacity, food and habitat become scarce, diseases and competition increase, causing the population to stabilize. In 1944, 29 reindeer were released on St. Matthew Island (Alaska); by 1963, they had increased to about 6,000, overgrazing lichens, and nearly all starved after one winter.

cau_hoi: According to the principle of Russian scientist Georgy Gause (1934), what happens when two species compete for the exact same resource?
B: One species will prevail and eliminate the other
giai_thich: Gause cultured two species of paramecium in the same test tube and found that one species always eliminated the other. This is known as the competitive exclusion principle. In nature, coexisting species often 'partition' resources: they eat different foods, forage at different tree levels, or at different times. Each species has its own 'niche'.

cau_hoi: How did the Steller's sea cow, a giant relative of the manatee (dugong), go extinct?
A: Hunted to extinction just about 27 years after being discovered by Europeans in 1741
giai_thich: Steller's sea cows grew to about 8-9 meters long, weighing several tons, and lived around the Commander Islands in the Bering Sea. Naturalist Georg Steller described them in 1741 when Vitus Bering's expedition ship sank. They were slow, did not dive deeply, and were easily hunted by seal and otter hunters for their meat. By 1768, none remained.

cau_hoi: What is a region with many endemic species but has lost at least 70% of its original vegetation called in conservation?
giai_thich: The concept was proposed by British ecologist Norman Myers in 1988. There are currently about 36 hotspots, covering only about 2.5% of the land area but home to more than half of the endemic plant species. Vietnam is located in the Indo-Burma hotspot (India – Myanmar). Other examples include Madagascar, the Atlantic Forest in Brazil, and the Mediterranean region.

cau_hoi: Which terrestrial ecosystem has the highest species diversity in the world?
giai_thich: Tropical rainforests cover only about 6% of the Earth's land surface but likely contain more than half of all terrestrial species. Scientist Terry Erwin once estimated that a single tree in Panama could host hundreds of beetle species. The warm, humid climate year-round, with no winter, along with multiple canopy layers, creates countless different ecological niches.

cau_hoi: Why do humans, pigs, or cattle tend to survive better on larger islands than on smaller ones, according to the island biogeography theory?
C: Larger islands have more habitats, larger populations, so they are less likely to go extinct; islands close to the mainland are more likely to receive new species
giai_thich: The island biogeography theory was proposed by Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson in 1967. The number of species on an island is a balance between the number of new arrivals and the number of extinctions. Larger islands and those closer to the mainland have more species. This theory also applies to forest areas fragmented into 'islands' among farmland, explaining why reserves should be large and connected.

cau_hoi: In a fish pond, when the tilapia population becomes too dense, what is their tendency?
B: Compete for food, grow slower, and become more susceptible to disease
giai_thich: High density leads to insufficient food and oxygen for all, excessive waste, and rapid disease spread. This is an example of intraspecific competition. In nature, intraspecific competition helps regulate population numbers; for example, many plant species self-thin: weaker plants are shaded and die off by stronger ones. Fish farmers need to stock at reasonable densities.

cau_hoi: What is a species that is only found in a specific geographic area and nowhere else in the world called?
giai_thich: Madagascar is a famous example: about 90% of the plants and nearly all lemur species here are endemic, as the island separated from the continent tens of millions of years ago. Vietnam has many endemic species such as the saola, white-cheeked gibbon, Cat Ba langur, and white-crowned pheasant. Endemic species in small areas are often very vulnerable to extinction.

cau_hoi: Which international convention controls the trade of wild animals and plants between countries?
giai_thich: CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora) was signed in 1973 in Washington and came into effect in 1975. Currently, there are about 185 members, with Vietnam joining in 1994. Species are classified into Appendix I (prohibited from trade for commercial purposes, such as tigers and rhinos), Appendix II, and III (controlled trade).

cau_hoi: Swedish scientist Svante Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2022 for what work?
A: Decoding the genome of Neanderthals and discovering Denisovans
giai_thich: Pääbo and his team managed to read DNA from bone fragments tens of thousands of years old, despite ancient DNA being easily damaged and mixed with modern DNA. In 2010, they published the Neanderthal genome and discovered Denisovans from just a finger bone fragment found in Siberia. The results show that modern non-Africans carry about 1-2% Neanderthal DNA. This field of science is called paleogenetics.

cau_hoi: In 2004, scientists announced the discovery of a small ancient human species about 1 meter tall found on the island of Flores (Indonesia), what is its nickname?
giai_thich: Homo floresiensis was only about 1.1 meters tall, with a brain the size of a chimpanzee, yet still made stone tools. They lived in Liang Bua cave until about 50,000 years ago. Scientists believe the small size may be an example of the "island rule." The island of Flores also had dwarf elephants (Stegodon) and Komodo dragons. The discovery indicates that many human species once coexisted.

cau_hoi: The fossil "Toumaï" (Sahelanthropus tchadensis), about 7 million years old, was found in which country in 2001?
giai_thich: Toumaï means "hope of life" in the local Goran language, a name often given to children born in the dry season. The skull was found in the Djurab desert, far west of the Rift Valley, surprising scientists who previously thought human ancestors only lived in East Africa. This is one of the oldest candidates on the evolutionary branch of humans after splitting from chimpanzees.

cau_hoi: In 2015, paleoanthropologist Lee Berger announced a newly discovered ancient human species found deep in Rising Star cave (South Africa). What is this species?
giai_thich: To enter the Dinaledi chamber, scientists had to squeeze through a narrow gap of only about 18 cm, so Berger recruited small-bodied scientists, including many women. They found over 1,500 bone fragments from at least 15 individuals. Homo naledi had a small brain but lived relatively recently, about 335,000 – 236,000 years ago. The name "naledi" means "star" in Sesotho.

cau_hoi: The strange soft-bodied, disc-shaped, leaf-shaped organisms that lived about 575 – 538 million years ago, before the Cambrian explosion, are called what, named after a hill range in Australia?
giai_thich: The fossils were discovered by geologist Reg Sprigg in 1946 in the Ediacara Hills, South Australia. These were the first large multicellular organisms, such as Dickinsonia, which had a disc shape with stripes. In 2018, scientists found cholesterol molecules in Dickinsonia fossils, proving it was an animal. Most Ediacaran organisms have no clear relatives among today's animals.

cau_hoi: The "Red Queen" hypothesis in evolution, named after the story "Alice in Wonderland," discusses what?
A: Every species has a king and queen
B: Species stop evolving when they are strong enough
C: Species that are red live longer
D: Species must continuously evolve just to maintain their position in the race against enemies, parasites, and competitors
giai_thich: In the story, the Red Queen tells Alice: "Here, you must run as fast as you can just to stay in the same place." Biologist Leigh Van Valen used this imagery in 1973. For example, if rabbits run faster, then foxes also select to run faster; if bacteria become drug-resistant, humans must find new drugs. This hypothesis also helps explain why sexual reproduction is common.

cau_hoi: Striped snakes in North America can eat rough-skinned newts that contain the extremely potent toxin tetrodotoxin. This is an example of which phenomenon?
giai_thich: A rough-skinned newt is toxic enough to kill many adult humans, but in some areas, striped snakes have evolved resistance to the toxin due to mutations in sodium channels. In places where snakes are strongly resistant, newts are also more toxic, creating an "arms race." Snakes pay a price: after eating newts, they move sluggishly for hours. This is a classic example of co-evolution.

cau_hoi: Cheetahs have an unusually high genetic similarity among individuals. Scientists explain this phenomenon by which effect?
B: Bottleneck effect: the population once decreased to very few individuals
C: Due to eating the same type of food
giai_thich: About 10,000 – 12,000 years ago, at the end of the Ice Age, the cheetah population drastically declined, leaving only a few surviving individuals. The genetic diversity was so low that skin grafts between unrelated cheetahs sometimes were not rejected. As a result, they are more susceptible to diseases and have a high rate of abnormal sperm. The northern elephant seal, which was down to just a few dozen individuals in 1890, is another example.

cau_hoi: When a small group of individuals leaves the original population to establish a new population, the gene frequency of the new population may differ significantly from the original population. What is this phenomenon called?
giai_thich: A group of people or animals that migrate only carries a small portion of the genetic variants from the original population, so a rare variant can become common. For example, the Amish in Pennsylvania (USA), originating from about 200 individuals, have a high rate of a rare disease causing extra fingers. The founder effect is a form of genetic drift, the random change in gene frequency.

cau_hoi: The formation of a new species when a population is divided by mountains, rivers, or seas, and each group evolves separately is called what?
giai_thich: When the Isthmus of Panama emerged about 3 million years ago, the populations of snapping shrimp on either side were separated. Today, the shrimp that appear similar on the Pacific and Caribbean coasts no longer interbreed when brought together. Squirrels on either side of the Grand Canyon (USA) have also diverged. Geographic isolation is the most common pathway for speciation.

cau_hoi: The Arctic tern was once used as an example of a "ring species." What is a ring species?
A: A species living on a ring-shaped island
B: A species with a colored ring around its neck
C: A chain of populations surrounding an area, where adjacent populations can interbreed but the ends of the chain cannot
giai_thich: A more famous example is the Ensatina salamanders around California's Central Valley and the greenish warblers around the Tibetan Plateau. A ring species shows how a "new species" can gradually form across space, as if we see evolutionary steps lined up next to each other. Later DNA studies revealed that the tern example is more complex than the simple ring model.

cau_hoi: Why are populations with few individuals, such as the Cat Ba langur with only a few dozen to over a hundred individuals, more susceptible to extinction?
A: Because they prefer to be alone
B: Low genetic diversity, leading to inbreeding, and a random disaster can wipe out the entire population
giai_thich: Small populations face the "extinction vortex": inbreeding makes offspring weak, diseases, floods, or a few being poached can have a large impact. The Cat Ba langur is an endemic primate that only lives on Cat Ba Island (Hai Phong), which had dwindled to about 50 individuals in the early 2000s. Thanks to strict protection, their numbers are gradually increasing.

cau_hoi: In evolution, how long ago did the "most recent common ancestor" of humans and chimpanzees live?
giai_thich: Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees; both evolved from a common ancestor. The human and chimp genomes are about 98 – 99% similar when comparing corresponding DNA segments. One notable difference: humans have 46 chromosomes, while chimpanzees have 48, because human chromosome 2 was formed by the fusion of two chromosomes from their ancestor.

cau_hoi: Which of the following features helps identify a fossil of a human ancestor that walked on two legs?
A: The foramen magnum (the hole in the skull connecting to the spine) is located underneath, at the center of the skull
giai_thich: In bipedal species, the spine connects directly from the base of the skull, so the foramen magnum is located at the center of the skull's base. In chimpanzees and other quadrupedal species, this hole is shifted towards the back. A short and wide pelvis, inward-angled thigh bones, and a parallel big toe are also indicators. The Laetoli footprints in Tanzania, about 3.66 million years old, are the best direct evidence.

cau_hoi: In which country did scientists find the fossil of a whale with legs, such as Pakicetus (about 50 million years ago), indicating that whale ancestors lived on land?
giai_thich: Pakicetus was about the size of a dog, walked on four legs, but had inner ear structures characteristic of whales. Its name means "whale from Pakistan." Later fossils like Ambulocetus ("walking whale") and Rodhocetus show that legs gradually shortened, and bodies adapted to the sea. In Egypt's "Valley of Whales" (Wadi Al-Hitan), there are fossils of Basilosaurus with tiny hind limbs.

cau_hoi: Today, horses have one toe (hoof), but what were their ancestors like about 55 million years ago?
D: Small like dogs, had multiple toes, lived in forests
giai_thich: The early ancestors of horses, often referred to as Eohippus (or Hyracotherium), were only about 30 – 60 cm tall, with four toes on the front legs and three on the back, feeding on leaves in forests. As the climate became drier and grasslands expanded, horse species grew larger, legs elongated for speed, and the number of toes gradually decreased. The fossil record of horses is one of the most thoroughly studied pieces of evidence for evolution.

cau_hoi: Why do the human arm, bat wing, whale fin, and cat foreleg have similar bone structures despite different functions?
A: Because they live in the same place
C: They are homologous organs, inherited from a common ancestor
D: Because they eat the same type of food
giai_thich: All have one upper arm bone, two forearm bones, wrist bones, and finger bones. In bats, the fingers elongate to stretch the wing membrane; in whales, the bones shorten to form a fin. Darwin argued that there is no reason for a "designer" to use the same skeleton for different tasks unless they share a common origin. In contrast, bird wings and butterfly wings are analogous structures.

cau_hoi: What method helps scientists determine the age of fossils millions of years old?
C: Measuring radioactive isotopes in the volcanic rock layers above and below the fossil
giai_thich: Some radioactive elements like potassium-40 decay into argon-40 at a constant rate, so they can be used as a "clock." Potassium-40 has a half-life of about 1.25 billion years, suitable for dating rocks millions of years old. The carbon-14 method can only be used for samples under about 50,000 years, so it is not applicable to dinosaur bones. Lucy's age was determined thanks to volcanic ash layers.

cau_hoi: Which plant was used in a classic experiment showing that plants of the same species at different altitudes have different shapes, partly due to genes and partly due to the environment?
A: Rice plants in the Red River Delta
D: Yarrow (Achillea) on the Sierra Nevada mountains, California
giai_thich: In the 1940s, scientists Clausen, Keck, and Hiesey collected yarrow from various altitudes and planted them in the same garden. Plants from high-altitude regions remained shorter even when grown in the plains, indicating that the differences have a genetic basis, resulting from local adaptation. This is a stepping stone on the path to forming a new species.

cau_hoi: According to scientists, how long ago did life on Earth likely appear?
A: About 3.5 billion years ago or earlier
giai_thich: The Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago. The earliest evidence widely accepted is the layered rock formations created by cyanobacteria (stromatolites) approximately 3.5 billion years old in Western Australia. For the next 2 billion years, life consisted only of single-celled microorganisms. Today, living stromatolites can still be found in Shark Bay, Western Australia.

cau_hoi: "The Great Oxygenation Event" about 2.4 billion years ago signifies what?
B: Cyanobacteria photosynthesized, causing oxygen to accumulate in the atmosphere for the first time
giai_thich: Cyanobacteria release oxygen during photosynthesis. Initially, oxygen was absorbed by iron in the oceans, creating the banded iron formations that humans mine today for iron ore. As oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere, many anaerobic microorganisms died off. However, oxygen also paved the way for organisms that use oxygen to generate more energy, leading to the emergence of animals.

cau_hoi: Tilapia, catfish, rice, chicken... in Vietnam all have new high-yield varieties. What is the downside of planting only a few identical varieties over a wide area?
A: Too many colors in the plants
D: Low genetic diversity means a single disease can devastate an entire region
giai_thich: The Irish Potato Famine (1845 – 1849) is a famous lesson: people primarily planted one potato variety, and when a blight struck, nearly the entire crop failed, resulting in about 1 million deaths. The Gros Michel banana variety was also nearly wiped out by Panama disease in the mid-20th century. Therefore, gene banks preserve many traditional crop varieties.

cau_hoi: Where is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, which stores the world's crop seeds, located?
A: Inside a mountain in the Svalbard archipelago (Norway), near the Arctic
B: At the bottom of the Pacific Ocean
giai_thich: The vault opened in 2008, dug deep into the rock in a permafrost region, keeping seeds at around −18°C. It stores over 1.2 million seed samples from most countries as a "backup" in case of disasters. In 2015, Syrian scientists withdrew seeds from the vault for the first time to replace a gene bank affected by war in Aleppo.

cau_hoi: What common plant symbolizes the "revival" of the ecosystem in the Chernobyl nuclear disaster area (1986)?
C: There are no plants; in fact, wildlife like wolves, deer, and Przewalski's horse have thrived in the exclusion zone
giai_thich: After humans evacuated from the exclusion zone of about 2,600 km², many wildlife species like wolves, moose, wild boars, and lynxes increased, even though radiation still harmed individuals. Przewalski's horse, a rare wild horse species, was released into this area in 1998 and has bred. This shows that human presence can have a stronger impact than radiation.

cau_hoi: Why is the Pacific salmon beneficial for riverbank forests after swimming upstream to spawn and then dying?
A: Because the fish makes the river water sweeter
B: Fish carcasses bring nutrients from the sea into the forest through bears, birds, and microorganisms
C: Because the fish eat all the insects
D: Because the fish turn into trees
giai_thich: Bears catch salmon and often bring them into the forest, eating only part and leaving the rest. The decaying fish provide nitrogen from the ocean to the soil. Scientists have measured traces of nitrogen isotopes "from the sea" in the leaves of spruce trees along rivers with salmon, and the trees there grow faster. This is a beautiful example of the connection between ecosystems.

cau_hoi: In 2010, the last Javan rhino in Vietnam was poached and killed in which national park?
giai_thich: The Javan rhino once lived in many Southeast Asian countries. A small population was rediscovered in the Cat Loc area (now part of Cat Tien National Park) in 1988. In 2010, the carcass of the last rhino was found with its horn cut off, and in 2011 conservation organizations declared the species extinct in Vietnam. Currently, only about 50 – 80 Javan rhinos remain in Ujung Kulon National Park (Indonesia).

cau_hoi: Why does Australia have so many marsupials like kangaroos, koalas, and wombat bears, while they are almost absent in other continents?
A: Australia separated from other continents a long time ago, allowing marsupials to evolve separately with little competition from placental mammals
giai_thich: Australia separated from Antarctica about 35 – 45 million years ago, carrying some marsupials with it. Isolated, they radiated and adapted into many forms: "marsupial wolves," "marsupial moles," "flying squirrels," similar to placental mammals elsewhere. In South America, marsupials still exist, such as opossums, and one species has even spread to North America.

cau_hoi: The Paris Agreement on climate (2015) aims to keep the Earth's temperature increase to no more than how much compared to pre-industrial times?
B: Below 2°C, striving for no more than 1.5°C
giai_thich: The agreement was adopted by nearly 200 countries at the COP21 conference in Paris in 2015. Scientists believe that every tenth of a degree is important: at 1.5°C, about 70 – 90% of tropical coral reefs could be lost, while at 2°C, the figure is over 99%. Global temperatures have already risen by about 1.2 – 1.3°C, and 2024 is projected to be the first year to exceed 1.5°C for the entire year.

cau_hoi: The northern elephant seal was once down to about 20 – 100 individuals by the end of the 19th century. How are they doing today?
D: Increased to over 200,000 individuals but with very low genetic diversity
giai_thich: Elephant seals were hunted for their blubber to make oil. Thanks to protection from Mexico and the U.S. since the early 20th century, their numbers have rebounded strongly. However, since all are descendants of a few dozen surviving individuals, they have very low genetic diversity compared to southern elephant seals. This is a classic example of the bottleneck effect: numbers can recover, but genetic diversity takes a long time to restore.

cau_hoi: In 1796, which French scientist proved that the woolly mammoth is different from modern elephants, thus confirming that species can go extinct?
giai_thich: Before Cuvier, many believed that species never went extinct, and that strange bones must belong to animals still living in unexplored regions. By meticulously comparing jaw bones, Cuvier demonstrated that the woolly mammoth and the 'Ohio elephant' (mastodon) were extinct species. He is considered the father of paleontology, but he opposed Lamarck's theory of evolution.

cau_hoi: Which British fossil collector, living in Lyme Regis, discovered the first complete ichthyosaur skeleton at around 12 years old?
giai_thich: In 1811 – 1812, Mary Anning and her brother Joseph discovered the ichthyosaur skeleton (fish lizard). She later found the first nearly complete plesiosaur skeleton and the first pterosaur in England. As a woman from a poor background, she was not admitted to the Geological Society of London. It is believed that the English tongue twister 'She sells seashells by the seashore' was inspired by her.

cau_hoi: Which British scientist coined the term 'Dinosauria' (terrible lizard) in 1842?
giai_thich: Owen named it based on three known genera: Megalosaurus, Iguanodon, and Hylaeosaurus. He also founded the Natural History Museum in London. Owen was a distinguished anatomist but vehemently opposed Darwin's theory. In 1854, the world's first dinosaur statues were erected in Crystal Palace Park (London) under his guidance, and they still exist today.

cau_hoi: Who is referred to as 'Darwin's bulldog' for passionately defending the theory of evolution in debates?
giai_thich: In 1860 at Oxford, Huxley debated Bishop Samuel Wilberforce. According to anecdotes, Wilberforce asked Huxley whether his grandfather or grandmother was descended from monkeys, and Huxley replied that he would rather have a monkey for an ancestor than a man who used his talents to obscure the truth. Huxley was also the first to strongly propose that birds are related to dinosaurs.

cau_hoi: Who coined the phrase 'survival of the fittest'?
giai_thich: The English philosopher Herbert Spencer used this phrase in 1864, and Darwin included it in the fifth edition of 'On the Origin of Species' in 1869. 'Fittest' here does not mean the strongest or largest, but the most suited to the environment, leaving the most offspring. A small, slow animal that is well camouflaged can still be the 'fittest'.

cau_hoi: Which book by Thomas Malthus on population inspired both Darwin and Wallace to think of the idea of natural selection?
C: "An Essay on the Principle of Population" (1798)
giai_thich: Malthus argued that population tends to increase faster than food supply, leading to competition and famine. Darwin read the book in 1838 and realized that in nature, organisms produce more offspring than can survive, so only those with favorable traits persist. Wallace also recalled Malthus while suffering from malaria in 1858.

cau_hoi: What did Charles Lyell's book 'Principles of Geology', which Darwin took on the Beagle, help Darwin understand?
A: The Earth is very old and small changes accumulate over long periods to create significant changes
B: The Earth is only a few thousand years old
giai_thich: Lyell developed the idea of James Hutton that slow processes like erosion, deposition, and volcanism happening today are the same ones that shaped the landscape in the past. Darwin applied this thinking to organisms: small changes over millions of years can create new species. In Chile, Darwin witnessed the coastline rising after an earthquake in 1835.

cau_hoi: Before publishing 'On the Origin of Species', Darwin spent about 8 years meticulously studying which group of animals?
B: Barnacles, a type of crustacean that attaches to rocks and ship hulls
giai_thich: From 1846 to 1854, Darwin studied nearly every known species of barnacle, writing four volumes. His son once asked a family friend: 'Where does your father study barnacles?', thinking all fathers did the same. This work helped Darwin gain deep insights into variation among individuals and classification, while also earning him respect in the scientific community before publishing his controversial ideas.

cau_hoi: The famous quote 'Nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution' (1973) is attributed to whom?
giai_thich: Dobzhansky was a Ukrainian-born geneticist living in the U.S., famous for his research on fruit flies. He was one of the architects of the 'Modern Synthesis' in the 1930s – 1940s, combining Darwin's natural selection with Mendel's genetics. The quote emphasizes that evolution is the thread that connects all fields of biology.

cau_hoi: The theory of 'punctuated equilibrium' proposed by Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould in 1972 suggests what?
B: Species often remain stable for long periods, then change relatively quickly during short bursts
C: Evolution always occurs steadily at a constant rate
giai_thich: The two paleontologists noted that in fossils, many species remain almost unchanged for millions of years, while new species often appear 'suddenly'. They suggested that new species often form rapidly in small, isolated populations, leaving few intermediate fossils. 'Rapid' here still means tens of thousands of years, which is short compared to geological time.

cau_hoi: What theory about evolution at the molecular level was proposed by Japanese geneticist Motoo Kimura in 1968?
A: Neutral theory of evolution: most changes in DNA are neutral and spread randomly
giai_thich: Kimura argued that many mutations are neither beneficial nor harmful, and their fate is determined by genetic drift rather than natural selection. This idea explains why DNA accumulates changes at a relatively constant rate, allowing it to be used as a "molecular clock" to estimate when two species diverged. This theory complements, rather than replaces, natural selection.

cau_hoi: Who coined the term "ecology" in 1866?
giai_thich: German zoologist Ernst Haeckel combined the Greek words "oikos" (house) and "logos" (study), meaning the science of the "house" of organisms. Haeckel was also a talented artist, famous for his book "Art Forms in Nature" depicting beautiful jellyfish and radiolarians. However, some of his embryonic drawings were criticized for being overly "beautified."

cau_hoi: In what year did British ecologist Arthur Tansley popularize the term "ecosystem"?
giai_thich: Tansley used the term "ecosystem" to refer to all organisms along with their physical environment, such as soil, water, and climate, forming a unified system. Previously, scientists often only referred to biological communities. This idea helps to view the flow of energy and the cycling of materials like water, carbon, and nitrogen through both organisms and the environment.

cau_hoi: In 1966, ecologist Robert Paine removed all starfish (Pisaster) from a rocky area in Washington State (USA). What was the result?
D: Mussels proliferated and dominated the rocky area, leading to a sharp decline in species
giai_thich: Starfish eat mussels. When there were no starfish, mussels grew unchecked, occupying the space of algae, snails, and clams, and the number of species in the experimental area dropped from 15 to about 8. From this experiment, Paine introduced the concept of "keystone species" in 1969, similar to a keystone that holds an arch together. The experiment demonstrated that predators can help maintain biodiversity.

cau_hoi: The famous graph showing the steady increase of CO₂ concentration in the atmosphere, with seasonal sawtooth fluctuations, has been measured since 1958 where?
giai_thich: The Keeling Curve is named after scientist Charles David Keeling. Mauna Loa was chosen because it is located in the Pacific Ocean, far from pollution sources, allowing for well-mixed air. The sawtooth pattern is due to the Northern Hemisphere having more land: in summer, vegetation absorbs CO₂, causing a decrease in concentration, while in winter, leaves fall and decompose, causing an increase, as if the Earth is "breathing."

cau_hoi: The population of snowshoe hares and Canadian lynxes fluctuates in a cycle of about 10 years. Where does the classic data on this phenomenon come from?
B: Hudson Bay Company fur purchase records
giai_thich: The Hudson Bay Company recorded the number of pelts purchased from hunters for nearly 100 years, dating back to the 19th century. When hares are abundant, lynxes have plenty of prey and increase in number; when lynxes are abundant, hares are eaten and food becomes scarce, leading to a decline; then lynxes also starve and decrease in number. The Lotka-Volterra mathematical model describes predator-prey relationships in this way.

cau_hoi: Organisms that produce many offspring, grow quickly, and provide little care like mice, fish, and insects are classified under which reproductive strategy?
giai_thich: r-strategy species "bet on numbers," suitable for fluctuating environments, such as cod that lay millions of eggs. K-strategy species like elephants, whales, humans, and orangutans have fewer offspring, provide extensive care, and live long, suitable for stable environments near carrying capacity. Female orangutans give birth to one offspring approximately every 7-8 years, so populations recover very slowly when hunted.

cau_hoi: The phenomenon where some species have difficulty finding mates and defending themselves in groups when their numbers are too low, leading to even faster declines, is called what?
giai_thich: American ecologist Warder Clyde Allee described this phenomenon in the 1930s. The passenger pigeon is a possible example: they lived in huge flocks, and when their numbers decreased, group breeding became ineffective. The collapse of the cod fishery off Newfoundland in 1992 also recovered slower than expected. Therefore, conservation needs to act before populations drop too low.

cau_hoi: According to ecologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson (1957), what is the "niche" of a species?
B: The number of individuals of the species
C: All the conditions and resources that the species needs to survive and reproduce
giai_thich: The niche includes temperature, humidity, food, habitat, activity time, etc. Hutchinson likened it to a "multidimensional space." The habitat is the "address" of the species, while the niche is like a "profession." Ecologist Robert MacArthur discovered in 1958 that 5 species of warblers in North America coexist on the same type of pine tree but forage in different parts of the tree.

cau_hoi: The phenomenon of many female elephants in Gorongosa National Park (Mozambique) giving birth without tusks after the civil war is an example of what?
C: Elephants lack calcium in their diet
D: Poaching for tusks creates very strong selective pressure on elephants
giai_thich: During the civil war (1977-1992), about 90% of elephants were killed, mainly for their tusks. Female elephants without tusks were less hunted, so they survived and reproduced. The proportion of tuskless females increased from about 18.5% to about 51%. A 2021 study found the related gene located on the X chromosome. This is an example showing that humans can cause evolution to occur very rapidly.

cau_hoi: In 1971, scientists released 10 Italian wall lizards on the small island of Pod Mrčaru (Croatia). About 36 years later, what did they discover?
C: The lizards switched to eating more plants and had larger heads, with intestines that developed valves to help digest leaves
giai_thich: In a study in 2008, the dense population on the island was confirmed to be descendants of those released, thanks to DNA analysis. They had larger heads, stronger bites, and notably had cecal valves, a structure in the intestines that helps ferment leaves, which is very rare in this species. This is an example of rapid evolution observed in just a few decades.

cau_hoi: On the island of Kauai (Hawaii), in just about 20 generations, most male crickets became "deaf" and could not chirp. Why?
A: A parasitic fly listens for chirping to lay eggs on crickets, so non-chirping crickets survive more
giai_thich: The parasitic fly Ormia listens for cricket sounds to find them, and its larvae burrow in and eat the crickets from the inside. A mutation flattened the wings of male crickets, losing the sound-producing part, and spread rapidly from the early 2000s. Deaf crickets still find mates by standing near chirping males. Later, scientists also discovered a new type of "chirping" crickets.

cau_hoi: John Endler's experiment with guppies in Trinidad showed what?
A: Fish change color according to the moonlight
D: In streams with many predators, male fish are less colorful; when moved to streams with fewer enemies, they gradually became more colorful over several generations
giai_thich: Female fish prefer brightly colored males (sexual selection), but bright colors also make fish more vulnerable to predation (natural selection). In the 1970s – 1980s, Endler created experimental ponds and moved fish upstream to areas with fewer predators. After about 15 generations, the males had significantly more spots. The experiment showed that two selective forces are in conflict.

cau_hoi: The Culex mosquitoes living in the London Underground are considered by some scientists as an example of what?
B: A population that has adapted specifically to the underground environment and hardly interbreeds with mosquitoes above ground
giai_thich: The underground mosquitoes feed on human and rat blood, are active year-round, do not hibernate, and mate in confined spaces, unlike their relatives above ground that primarily feed on bird blood. There was a hypothesis that they evolved in the tunnels in just over a hundred years, but DNA studies in 2024 showed that this mosquito form has a much older origin, possibly from the Middle East, associated with the first agricultural civilizations.

cau_hoi: The first confirmed dinosaur fossil with feathers (down-like feathers), published in 1996 in Liaoning (China), is called what?
giai_thich: Sinosauropteryx is a small carnivorous dinosaur, about 1 meter long, with a layer of down on its back and tail. In 2010, scientists found pigment sacs (melanosomes) in its feathers and suggested that its tail had brown and white stripes, like a cat's tail. Later, Liaoning produced a series of feathered dinosaur fossils, strongly reinforcing the idea that birds evolved from dinosaurs.

cau_hoi: The dinosaur Microraptor, found in China, has what unusual characteristic?
B: It lived in the deep sea
C: It is as big as a whale
D: It has long feathers on both arms and legs, resembling having four wings
giai_thich: Microraptor was less than 1 meter long and lived about 120 million years ago. The flying feathers on both its front and back legs suggest it could glide between trees. Pigment studies in 2012 showed its feathers were iridescent black like a crow's. Microraptor suggests that the evolution of flight in dinosaurs and birds may have gone through various experiments.

cau_hoi: Lystrosaurus, a reptile resembling a pig-sized mammal, is famous for what?
C: It survived the mass extinction at the end of the Permian and became the most common land animal afterward
giai_thich: After the Great Extinction about 252 million years ago, Lystrosaurus dominated the land, in some places accounting for about 90% of vertebrate animal fossils. They likely survived due to their moderate size, burrowing habits, ability to eat a variety of plants, and rapid reproduction. Fossils of Lystrosaurus found in South Africa, India, and Antarctica are evidence that the continents were once connected.

cau_hoi: The dinosaur Spinosaurus, with a large sail on its back, is famous for what ecological characteristic?
A: It is a carnivorous dinosaur adapted to aquatic life, eating fish
giai_thich: The first fossil was found by German paleontologist Ernst Stromer in Egypt in 1912, but was destroyed when a bomb hit the museum in Munich in 1944. In 2014 and 2020, new fossils in Morocco showed it had a paddle-like tail, dense bones for diving, and nostrils positioned towards the back. Scientists still debate whether it swam well or primarily waded through water hunting fish like a heron.

cau_hoi: The geological epoch proposed by humans called the "Anthropocene" signifies what?
B: Humans have become a force changing the Earth equivalent to geological processes
giai_thich: The term was popularized by chemist Paul Crutzen (Nobel 1995) in 2000. The traces left by humans in future rocks include plastics, concrete, chicken bones, and radioactive materials from nuclear bomb tests. However, in 2024, the International Union of Geological Sciences voted not to recognize the Anthropocene as an official unit in the geological time scale, although the term is still widely used.

cau_hoi: The "Kunming – Montreal" framework on biodiversity in 2022 aims for what famous goal?
C: To protect at least 30% of Earth's land and marine areas by 2030
D: To plant one tree for each person
giai_thich: The "30x30" goal was adopted by nearly 200 countries at the COP15 conference of the Convention on Biological Diversity, hosted by China but held in Montreal (Canada). At that time, only about 17% of land and 8% of oceans were protected. The framework also aims to restore 30% of degraded ecosystems and halve the rate of introduction of invasive species.

cau_hoi: What happened to the bright golden toad that only lives in the Monteverde cloud forest (Costa Rica) after 1989?
A: It has not been seen again and was declared extinct in 2004
giai_thich: The golden toad was described in 1966, with males having a bright orange-yellow color as if painted. In 1987, scientists counted about 1,500 individuals at breeding pools, but by 1988-1989 only a few were seen, and the last one was recorded on May 15, 1989. Possible causes include unusual drought related to El Niño, climate change, and fungal disease. This is one of the first species believed to be affected by climate change.

cau_hoi: In 1980, what evidence did Luis and Walter Alvarez provide for the asteroid hypothesis causing dinosaur extinction?
D: A thin layer of clay containing a lot of iridium, rare on Earth but common in meteorites
giai_thich: The boundary layer between the Cretaceous and Paleogene periods found in Gubbio (Italy), Denmark, and New Zealand contained iridium levels tens of times higher than normal. Luis Alvarez was a Nobel Prize-winning physicist, and his son Walter was a geologist. Initially, many were skeptical, but by 1990-1991, a massive impact crater was identified in the Yucatán, confirming the hypothesis.

cau_hoi: What is the main cause believed to be behind the mass extinction at the end of the Ordovician period, about 445 million years ago?
C: A sudden ice age causing sea levels to drop and temperatures to cool
giai_thich: At that time, most life was underwater. As the supercontinent Gondwana drifted closer to Antarctica, glaciers formed, and sea levels dropped from warm shallow seas, which were home to the most organisms. About 85% of marine species disappeared. Some scientists also believe that the spread of terrestrial plants may have absorbed CO₂, contributing to the cooling of the Earth.

cau_hoi: What geological event is associated with the mass extinction at the end of the Triassic period, about 201 million years ago, and what were its consequences?
C: The Moon colliding with the Earth
D: Large volcanic eruptions as the supercontinent Pangaea began to break apart, allowing dinosaurs to dominate
giai_thich: Eruptions in the "Central Atlantic Magmatic Province" covered areas now part of the Americas, Africa, and Europe as the Atlantic Ocean began to open. CO₂ levels rose sharply, causing the climate to warm and the oceans to acidify. Many groups of reptilian relatives of crocodiles, competitors of dinosaurs, were wiped out, paving the way for dinosaurs to dominate the Jurassic period.

cau_hoi: What hypothesis explains why the Carboniferous period (about 359 – 299 million years ago) produced a massive amount of coal?
B: Dead wood accumulated faster than it could decompose, possibly because wood-decaying fungi (lignin) were not yet widespread
giai_thich: Swamp forests with tree ferns and giant clubmosses were buried in oxygen-poor water, gradually turning into coal. The hypothesis about fungi is still debated; many scientists believe that the humid climate and vast lowlands were the main causes. During this period, oxygen levels in the atmosphere may have reached about 30-35%, allowing giant insects to exist. Most of the world's coal used today comes from this period.

cau_hoi: In 1995, what surprising result did Walter Gehring's team find when they inserted the mouse eye gene into fruit flies?
A: Flies grew extra fly eyes on their legs, wings, and antennae
giai_thich: The Pax6 gene in mice and the eyeless gene in flies are so similar that the mouse gene could still "command" fly cells to create eyes, but they were the compound eyes of flies. This shows that human eyes and insect eyes, despite their very different structures, share a common "master switch" from a common ancestor over 500 million years ago. The field of research combining development and evolution is called "evo-devo."

cau_hoi: What did the experiment by Russian geneticist Dmitry Belyaev, starting in 1959 with silver foxes, show?
D: By only selecting the tamest individuals for breeding, after several dozen generations, foxes became dog-like: wagging tails, floppy ears, spotted fur
giai_thich: Belyaev and later Lyudmila Trut selected foxes based on one criterion: less fear of humans. Surprisingly, many other traits also appeared simultaneously, such as floppy ears, curled tails, spotted fur, and short snouts, similar to the changes seen in dogs, pigs, and domestic cattle. This phenomenon is called "domestication syndrome," and the experiment continues in Novosibirsk.

cau_hoi: The Hawaiian honeycreeper bird group is a famous example of adaptive radiation. What is their biggest threat today?
A: Bird malaria spread by mosquitoes brought by humans
giai_thich: From a sparrow-like ancestor that arrived in Hawaii millions of years ago, over 50 species have evolved with various beak types: long curved beaks for nectar, thick beaks for seed stripping, and beaks like clamps. Mosquitoes arrived in Hawaii around 1826, bringing bird malaria. Many species now only survive in high, cold areas without mosquitoes. As the climate warms, mosquitoes are moving higher, so in 2023 Hawaii began releasing male mosquitoes carrying bacteria that prevent eggs from hatching.

cau_hoi: "Lonesome George," who died in 2012, is famous for what reason?
C: Being the last known giant tortoise of the subspecies on Pinta Island (Galápagos)
D: Being the oldest monkey in the world
giai_thich: George was discovered in 1971 when goats introduced by humans had eaten away the vegetation. Scientists searched for a mate for him for 40 years, but no eggs hatched. He died on June 24, 2012, likely over 100 years old. Afterward, goats were removed from Pinta Island, and tortoises from other islands were released to restore the ecosystem. George's body was preserved and displayed in Galápagos.

cau_hoi: In 1926, why did Australia release the Cactoblastis moth, and what was the result?
A: To kill mosquitoes; it was ineffective
B: To eliminate the invasive prickly pear cactus that had covered tens of millions of hectares; it was a resounding success
C: To pollinate coffee plants; it failed
giai_thich: The prickly pear cactus from the Americas spread over about 24 million hectares in Queensland and New South Wales.
