The larvae of the Cactoblastis moth from Argentina burrowed into the cactus stems, and within a few years, they had destroyed most of them. People even built a hall named Cactoblastis to honor it. However, when this moth spread to Florida (USA), it threatened native cactus species.

cau_hoi: The rinderpest disease was declared globally eradicated in 2011. How did this affect the Serengeti grasslands?
C: The wildebeest population surged, reducing dry grass and leading to fewer wildfires and regrowth of trees
giai_thich: Rinderpest is the second disease after smallpox to be completely eradicated by humans. When the disease was controlled in the Serengeti from the 1960s, the wildebeest population increased from about 250,000 to over 1 million. They grazed on grass, reducing large fires, allowing acacia trees to regrow, which in turn increased populations of lions, hyenas, and many other species. This is an example of how a pathogen can shape an entire ecosystem.

cau_hoi: Since the 1990s, the vulture population in India has decreased by over 95%. What is the main cause?
A: Due to a lack of carcasses
D: Vultures eating livestock carcasses containing the painkiller diclofenac, leading to kidney failure
giai_thich: Diclofenac is used for sick cattle. When the cattle die, vultures eat the carcasses and suffer mass kidney failure. With fewer vultures, livestock carcasses decompose longer, leading to a rise in feral dogs due to the surplus food, which in turn increases rabies. A 2024 study estimated that this collapse is linked to an additional half a million human deaths over five years. India banned the use of diclofenac in livestock in 2006.

cau_hoi: In 1958, a large-scale campaign to eradicate sparrows in China, believing they ate grain, resulted in what consequence?
A: Insects and locusts surged due to the loss of natural predators, causing greater crop damage
giai_thich: During the "Four Pests Campaign" (flies, mosquitoes, rats, sparrows), people banged pots and drums to prevent the birds from resting until they fell from exhaustion. Scientists later pointed out that sparrows eat a lot of insects. By 1960, sparrows were replaced by bedbugs on the list. This is a classic lesson about intervening in the food web without fully understanding the connections.

cau_hoi: Which snake, accidentally introduced to Guam after World War II, has wiped out most of the native forest bird species on the island?
giai_thich: The brown tree snake likely hid on military cargo ships from New Guinea. Without natural predators on Guam, the snake proliferated to densities of thousands per square kilometer in some areas. Most native forest bird species have disappeared. The lack of birds to disperse seeds has also affected Guam's forests. The snakes have also climbed power lines, causing frequent power outages. The U.S. once dropped poisoned dead mice from helicopters to kill the snakes.

cau_hoi: In Central America, some acacia trees with hollow thorns provide shelter and nectar for ants. How do the ants respond?
A: Attack leaf-eating animals and cut back surrounding vines and other plants
B: Cause the acacia tree to die
giai_thich: This is a famous example of mutualism studied by ecologist Daniel Janzen in the 1960s. The acacia also produces nutrient-rich "Belt bodies" at the leaf tips as food for the ants. When Janzen removed the ants, the acacia was overwhelmed by insects and other plants, leading to many trees dying. Some acacia trees in Africa have similar relationships, with ants even attacking elephants.

cau_hoi: The European cuckoo lays its eggs in the nests of other birds like reed warblers. What is this phenomenon, and how have reed warblers evolved to cope?
A: Mutualism; host birds are very happy
B: Competition; host birds leave far away
C: Predation; host birds eat cuckoo eggs
D: Parasitic breeding; host birds have learned to recognize and remove foreign eggs
giai_thich: Cuckoo chicks hatch early and push the host's eggs or chicks out of the nest, then are raised by the host parents as their own despite being much larger. To cope, host birds have evolved the ability to recognize foreign eggs; conversely, each cuckoo female lays eggs that resemble the color of the host's eggs they parasitize. This is an example of an evolutionary "arms race." In Vietnam, the koel also lays eggs in the nests of crows and starlings.

cau_hoi: Why are lichens used as a "biological indicator" for air quality?
B: Many lichen species are very sensitive to sulfur dioxide, so they disappear in polluted areas
C: Because lichens change color with the weather
D: Because lichens only grow in cities
giai_thich: Lichens absorb water and minerals directly from the air and rain, without a protective layer, so they accumulate pollutants. In heavily polluted areas, only a few resilient species remain, while in clean air, there are lichen species with hair-like forms. When the air in London and Paris became cleaner from the late 20th century, many lichen species returned to the city.

cau_hoi: When a whale dies and sinks to the deep ocean floor, what happens?
C: The whale carcass becomes an ecosystem supporting hundreds of species for decades
giai_thich: At the deep sea floor, where food is scarce, a whale carcass is like a "feast." First, sharks and scavengers eat the flesh; then, worms and crabs clean up the remaining parts; finally, bacteria decompose the fat in the bones, creating sulfur compounds that nourish chemosynthetic organisms, which can last for 50 years or more. The Osedax worm ("bone-eating") has no mouth and uses "roots" to bore into the bones.

cau_hoi: What role do scientists believe whale feces play in the ocean?
B: Bring iron and nitrogen from the depths to the surface, nourishing plankton and helping absorb CO₂
D: Make seawater dirty and kill all organisms
giai_thich: Whales dive deep to feed and then defecate near the surface, where there is light. The feces are rich in iron, a nutrient often lacking in the Southern Ocean, helping phytoplankton grow, nourishing mollusks and fish, and absorbing CO₂. This phenomenon is called the "whale pump." Therefore, excessive whaling in the 20th century may have made the ocean less fertile.

cau_hoi: According to Bergmann's rule, mammals of the same group living in cold regions often have what characteristic compared to their relatives in warm regions?
C: Larger body size to retain heat better
giai_thich: Larger animals have a smaller surface area-to-volume ratio, so they lose heat more slowly. For example, Siberian tigers (Amur) are larger than Sumatran tigers, and moose in the North are larger. The rule was proposed by German biologist Carl Bergmann in 1847. However, there are many exceptions, and species also have other ways to keep warm, such as thick fur and layers of fat.

cau_hoi: The fennec fox in the Sahara Desert has very large ears, while the Arctic fox has small, round ears. This is an example of which ecological rule?
giai_thich: According to Allen's Rule (1877), animals in cold regions have shorter ears, legs, and tails to reduce heat loss, while in hot regions, these parts are longer to dissipate heat. The fennec fox's ears can be up to about 15 cm long, with many blood vessels to help dissipate heat, and they also help hear insects under the sand. The desert cottontail has much longer ears than the Arctic hare.

cau_hoi: What major problem did the Biosphere 2 project in Arizona (USA), where 8 people lived in a giant sealed greenhouse from 1991 to 1993, encounter?
A: Oxygen levels gradually decreased to dangerous levels, requiring additional oxygen to be pumped in from outside
giai_thich: Oxygen levels dropped from about 21% to around 14%. The cause was microorganisms in the organic-rich soil consuming oxygen, while the CO₂ produced was absorbed by the concrete. Many pollinator insect species died, and ants and cockroaches thrived. Biosphere 2 demonstrated how difficult it is to create a self-sustaining artificial ecosystem, and we should appreciate "Biosphere 1", which is Earth.

cau_hoi: What is the main idea behind scientist James Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis proposed in the 1970s?
B: Life and the Earth's environment interact as a self-regulating system, maintaining conditions suitable for life
C: The Earth is a giant thinking organism
giai_thich: The name Gaia is the Earth Mother goddess in Greek mythology, suggested by writer William Golding. Lovelock, along with microbiologist Lynn Margulis, developed the idea. To illustrate, he used the "Daisyworld" model, where white and black daisies self-regulate the planet's temperature. Many evolutionary biologists criticized the hypothesis, but it spurred the field of "Earth system science".

cau_hoi: "Earth Overshoot Day" signifies what?
A: The founding day of the United Nations
B: The day with the most earthquakes
C: The day of the year when humanity has used up the amount of natural resources that the Earth can regenerate in a year
D: The day the Earth is closest to the Sun
giai_thich: The Global Footprint Network calculates this day annually. In recent years, it has fallen around late July to early August, meaning humanity is living as if there are about 1.7 Earths. In the early 1970s, this day fell at the end of December. If everyone lived like people in some wealthy countries, we would need 4 to 5 Earths.

cau_hoi: How was the Père David's deer (also known as the milu) from China saved from extinction?
A: A small herd was kept at Woburn Abbey (England) and later their descendants were returned to China
B: They survived in the Amazon rainforest
giai_thich: This species had gone extinct in the wild, existing only in the imperial gardens of China. French missionary Armand David introduced them to Europe in 1865. Floods in 1895 and war in 1900 decimated the herd in Beijing. The Duke of Bedford gathered the remaining individuals from European zoos to Woburn. In 1985, the deer were returned to China, and now there are thousands.

cau_hoi: In 1974, the Mauritius kestrel was considered the rarest bird in the world when only how many wild individuals were known?
giai_thich: DDT pesticides and deforestation pushed this small kestrel species to the brink. Conservationist Carl Jones began a program in 1979, removing eggs to allow the mother to lay more and incubating the eggs artificially. By the 2000s, the population increased to several hundred. This is one of the most successful species recovery stories, although the population later declined again and needs continued protection.

cau_hoi: In the late 19th century, Indian mongooses were released in Jamaica and Hawaii to control rats in sugarcane fields. Why did the plan fail?
B: Mongooses hunt during the day while rats are mostly active at night, so mongooses turned to eating birds, turtles, and native lizards
giai_thich: Mongooses were released in Jamaica in 1872 and Hawaii in 1883. They ate ground-nesting bird eggs, sea turtle eggs, and many reptiles, contributing to the extinction of some species in the Caribbean. Rats persisted because they could climb trees and were active at night. The lesson: using "natural enemies" for biological control needs careful study, or it may create a new invasive species.

cau_hoi: In 2018, South Georgia Island in the South Atlantic was declared to have achieved what major conservation milestone?
A: Rodent-free after the world's largest rat eradication campaign on the island
C: Became the place with the most elephants
giai_thich: Rats came to the island with whaling and sealing ships from the 18th to 19th centuries, eating the eggs and chicks of millions of seabirds. From 2011 to 2015, helicopters dropped rat poison over about 1,000 km². After thorough checks with sniffer dogs, the island was declared rat-free in 2018. Bird species like the South Georgia pipit have significantly increased.

cau_hoi: In 1980, the black robin in the Chatham Islands (New Zealand) was down to just 5 individuals, with only one female remaining. What was that female famously named?
giai_thich: Conservationist Don Merton moved the last individuals to a safe island and used a "nest exchange" trick: taking Old Blue's eggs for another bird species to incubate, allowing her to lay more. Old Blue lived to about 14 years, double the usual lifespan of the species. Today, about 250-300 black robins are descendants of her, so they have extremely low genetic diversity but still survive.

cau_hoi: In Australia, giant mammals like Diprotodon (a rhino-sized marsupial) disappeared about 40,000 to 50,000 years ago. What are the main hypotheses about the cause?
D: Due to humans hunting and burning forests, possibly combined with a dry climate
giai_thich: Diprotodon was the largest marsupial ever, weighing up to about 2.7 tons. At the same time, there were giant kangaroos standing 2 meters tall and the "marsupial lion" Thylacoleo. Their disappearance coincided with the arrival of humans in Australia. In the Americas, mammoths and giant ground sloths also disappeared after humans arrived. The extent of human and climate contributions is still debated.

cau_hoi: Some ecologists argue that avocados with large seeds are "outdated fruits". Why?
A: Avocado seeds may have once been dispersed by giant extinct mammals like the giant ground sloth.
B: Because small birds prefer to eat avocado seeds.
giai_thich: The idea of "outdated fruits" was proposed by ecologists Daniel Janzen and Paul Martin in 1982. No wild mammals in America today can swallow whole avocados and disperse the seeds far away. It is possible that species like the giant ground sloth and Gomphothere (relatives of elephants) used to do this. After their extinction, avocado trees likely survived partly due to human cultivation.

cau_hoi: Who discovered the "Java Man" (Homo erectus) fossil in Trinil, Indonesia, in 1891?
giai_thich: Dubois was a Dutch physician who joined the Dutch army just to go to the East Indies in search of the "missing link" between apes and humans. He found a skull cap, teeth, and thigh bone, naming it Pithecanthropus erectus ("upright ape man"). Many scientists at the time were skeptical, causing him to hide the fossils for many years. In 2014, a shell with a wavy engraving about 500,000 years old was also discovered in Trinil.

cau_hoi: In 2019, a new ancient human species was announced from the Callao Cave on the island of Luzon. What is that species?
giai_thich: Scientists found teeth, finger bones, and toe bones that are at least about 50,000 – 67,000 years old. The teeth are very small, and the toe bones are curved like those of tree-dwelling ancestors. Like the Flores people, the existence of this species on a remote island raises questions about how ancient humans crossed the sea. Southeast Asia was once home to many coexisting human species.

cau_hoi: "The Taung Child," the first Australopithecus fossil described in 1925, died from what cause according to a 2006 study?
giai_thich: Anatomist Raymond Dart in South Africa recognized that the skull of the 3-year-old child had a foramen magnum positioned underneath, indicating it walked on two legs. Initially, the scientific community mocked him because they believed human origins were in Europe or Asia. In 2006, Lee Berger pointed out that the injuries in the eye sockets were identical to claw marks left by today's African crowned eagles on their monkey prey.

cau_hoi: "Piltdown Man," the "missing link" fossil found in England in 1912, turned out to be what?
A: A hoax: a human skull fused with a orangutan jaw that had been stained.
C: The actual fossil of the oldest human.
giai_thich: In 1953, scientists used fluorine dating techniques and discovered that the bone fragments were of different ages. The molars were filed down to resemble human teeth. The Piltdown Man misled science for 40 years, causing many to underestimate real discoveries in Africa like the Taung Child. In 2016, DNA analysis suggested that the culprit was likely amateur archaeologist Charles Dawson.

cau_hoi: In 2009, scientists published the skeleton of "Ardi" (Ardipithecus ramidus) about 4.4 million years old. What surprised them about Ardi?
A: Ardi knew how to use fire.
B: Ardi walked on two legs on the ground but had a separated big toe for climbing trees.
C: Ardi was as big as a gorilla.
giai_thich: Ardi was found in the Afar region (Ethiopia), older than Lucy by about 1.2 million years. The research team spent about 15 years excavating and analyzing very fragile bones. The foot had a "big toe" that helped grasp branches, but the pelvis indicated it could walk upright. This suggests that the common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees likely did not resemble modern chimpanzees as many people think.

cau_hoi: What mysterious event happened to the "Peking Man" fossils found in Zhoukoudian in the 1920s – 1930s?
C: Disappeared in 1941 while being transported to avoid war and has never been found.
giai_thich: As the Pacific War was about to break out, the fossils were packed for transport to the U.S. but went missing, possibly because the ship sank or the crates were lost at the port. Fortunately, anatomist Franz Weidenreich made detailed plaster casts and descriptions, allowing scientists to continue studying them. The Peking Man belonged to the species Homo erectus.

cau_hoi: What hypothesis did anthropologist Richard Wrangham propose about the role of cooking in human evolution?
A: Fire was only used for warmth.
D: Cooked food is easier to digest, richer in energy, helping to shorten the intestines and enlarge the brain.
giai_thich: According to Wrangham, Homo erectus may have used fire about 1.8 million years ago, although solid evidence of cooking fires comes from later, such as the Wonderwerk Cave (South Africa) about 1 million years ago. Cooking helps absorb more energy from the same amount of food and reduces chewing time. Chimpanzees spend about 5 – 6 hours a day chewing, while humans need less than 1 hour.

cau_hoi: Biologist Edward O. Wilson proposed the "Half-Earth" idea in 2016. What is that idea?
A: Cut down half of the forests.
B: Send half of humanity to Mars.
C: Only live in the Northern Hemisphere.
D: Set aside about half of the Earth's surface for nature to protect most species.
giai_thich: Wilson, a leading expert on ants and the father of island biogeography theory, argued that only by protecting half of the area can about 85% of species be preserved. He passed away in 2021 at the age of 92. The current 30x30 goal is seen as a step towards that. Wilson also coined the term "biophilia," the innate human love for nature.

cau_hoi: In April 2025, the company Colossal Biosciences (USA) attracted attention by announcing the "resurrection" of the dire wolf species. What did they actually do?
A: Cloned from intact dire wolf cells.
C: Edited about 20 genes in gray wolf cells to create wolves with some characteristics of dire wolves.
giai_thich: Dire wolves went extinct about 10,000 years ago. Three wolf pups were born with thick white fur and larger bodies. Many scientists, including experts from the IUCN, believe that these are still genetically modified gray wolves, not the actual extinct species returning. The debate raises the question: should we invest in "resurrection" or protect living species that are about to disappear?

cau_hoi: The Italian sparrow has been confirmed by scientists as a rare example of which form of speciation in animals?
A: Speciation due to hybridization between two different species: house sparrow and Spanish sparrow
giai_thich: DNA analysis in 2011 showed that the Italian sparrow carries a mixed genotype from the house sparrow and the Spanish sparrow, likely formed when the house sparrow spread into Europe with agriculture. It now exists stably as a separate species. Hybrid speciation is more common in plants, such as modern wheat, which is the result of hybridization between three grass species. In animals, examples are rarer but are increasingly being discovered thanks to genome decoding.

cau_hoi: Darwin referred to the sudden appearance and rapid diversification of which group of plants in the fossil record as "an abominable mystery"?
giai_thich: Flowering plants appeared prominently in the fossil record during the Cretaceous period about 130 million years ago and quickly became dominant. Darwin wrote this phrase in a letter to botanist Joseph Hooker in 1879. Today, DNA analysis suggests their ancestors may have appeared even earlier. The evolution alongside pollinating insects is believed to be a reason for the success of flowering plants. There are currently about 300,000 species of flowering plants.

cau_hoi: Why is the fossil population of the Chengjiang biota in Yunnan (China), discovered in 1984, important?
B: It has the largest dinosaur eggs
C: It contains the oldest human fossils
D: It preserves detailed soft tissue of Cambrian organisms about 518 million years ago, earlier than the Burgess Shale
giai_thich: Paleontologist Hou Xianguang discovered the first fossils in the Miao Qian Mountain. The fine-grained mudstone preserved eyes, intestines, and gills. Among them are Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia, the earliest chordates, possibly distant ancestors of fish and humans. The area was recognized by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2012.

cau_hoi: Dimetrodon, a reptile with a sail on its back often featured in dinosaur toys, is actually more closely related to which group?
giai_thich: Dimetrodon lived about 295 – 272 million years ago, over 40 million years before the first dinosaurs. It belongs to the "synapsid" group, which has one temporal fenestra on each side of the skull, similar to the ancestors of mammals. Its teeth have differentiated into various types, and the name Dimetrodon means "two types of teeth." Therefore, in terms of relatives, Dimetrodon is closer to humans than to dinosaurs.

cau_hoi: How long ago did the giant shark Megalodon (Otodus megalodon) go extinct?
A: Still alive in the deep sea
giai_thich: Megalodon could reach lengths of about 15 – 20 m, with teeth over 17 cm long. It fed on whales, and scientists have found whale bones with megalodon bite marks. The causes of extinction may include cooling seas, changes in prey, and competition with ancestral great white sharks. There is no scientific evidence that megalodon is still alive; if it were, we would have seen new shed teeth and bite marks on whales.

cau_hoi: Titanoboa, the largest snake ever known, lived about 60 million years ago and was found in the Cerrejón coal mine in which country?
giai_thich: Titanoboa measured about 13 m long and weighed over 1 ton, living only a few million years after the extinction of the dinosaurs, in swampy rainforests. Since snakes are ectothermic animals, its gigantic size suggests that the tropical climate of that time was warmer than today, possibly averaging around 30 – 34°C annually. The fossils were published in 2009, found alongside giant turtles and crocodiles, which were likely its prey.

cau_hoi: British biologist J.B.S. Haldane is said to have remarked that if a creator exists, they must have a "special fondness" for which group of organisms?
giai_thich: Beetles are the most diverse group of animals known, with about 400,000 described species, accounting for about a quarter of all known animal species. There may be hundreds of thousands of undescribed species. Their hard front wings protect the hind wings and body, allowing them to survive in almost every environment. Haldane was also one of the founders of population genetics.

cau_hoi: "Shifting baseline syndrome," proposed by fisheries scientist Daniel Pauly in 1995, describes what?
C: Each generation considers the state of nature when they were young as "normal," thus failing to recognize the level of degradation over many generations
giai_thich: For example, young fishermen see an average catch as normal, while their grandparents caught much larger and more numerous fish. Photographs of fish caught in Key West (Florida) from the 1950s to 2007 show that fish are getting smaller, but the smiles of the fishermen remain the same. Understanding this helps set higher goals for nature restoration.

cau_hoi: According to WWF's Living Planet Report 2024, what has been the average decline in the size of monitored wild animal populations since 1970?
giai_thich: The Living Planet Index monitors nearly 35,000 populations of over 5,000 species of mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, and amphibians. The most significant declines are in Latin America – the Caribbean (about 95%) and in freshwater ecosystems (about 85%). Note that this figure does not mean that 73% of animal individuals have disappeared, but rather the average decline in the size of monitored populations.

cau_hoi: What warning was issued by a 2017 study in reserves in Germany (data from the Krefeld Entomological Society)?
B: The biomass of flying insects has decreased by more than 75% over about 27 years
giai_thich: Amateur entomologists set identical traps at 63 locations from 1989 to 2016 and weighed the collected insects. The decline was about 76%, reaching up to 82% in mid-summer, even in reserves. Possible causes include pesticides, habitat loss in surrounding agricultural areas, and climate change. Insects are a crucial food source and pollinators.

cau_hoi: A 2019 study published in Science estimated how many birds North America has lost since 1970?
C: About 3 billion birds, nearly 30% of the total
giai_thich: Surprisingly, most of the decline came from common species like sparrows, starlings, and warblers, not just rare species. Weather radar data also showed a decrease in nocturnal migratory birds. In contrast, waterfowl and raptors like eagles have increased due to wetland protection and DDT bans, indicating that conservation measures are effective.

cau_hoi: In 2019, what concerning discovery did scientists make about small crustaceans living in the Mariana Trench nearly 11 km deep?
B: They have microplastics in their intestines
D: They can swim to the surface
giai_thich: Scientists at Newcastle University (UK) collected amphipods from six of the deepest ocean trenches and found microplastics in their intestines in every trench, with a rate of up to 100% in the Mariana Trench. A new species was even named Eurythenes plasticus. This shows that plastic waste has infiltrated the most remote places on the planet.

cau_hoi: Lionfish, a beautiful venomous fish from the Indo-Pacific, is causing what problem in the Caribbean and Atlantic waters?
A: An invasive species that eats many native juvenile fish, threatening coral reefs
B: They are all eaten by sharks
C: They change the color of the water
giai_thich: Lionfish were likely released from aquariums in Florida in the 1980s. In their new environment, native fish do not recognize them as predators, and they have few natural enemies. A female can lay about 2 million eggs each year. Countries in the region encourage people to catch and process lionfish into dishes, as their meat is very tasty once the venomous spines are removed.

cau_hoi: How did the zebra mussel, a small bivalve from the Black Sea – Caspian Sea, invade the Great Lakes (North America) since 1988?
A: By being cultivated by humans for food
D: Through ballast water of ships from Europe
giai_thich: Ships take in water to balance, then discharge it at the port of arrival, carrying countless small organisms. Zebra mussels proliferate and clog the intake pipes of power plants and water treatment facilities, causing billions of dollars in damage. They filter water very effectively, making lakes clearer, but depriving plankton and fish of food. The international convention on ballast water management came into effect in 2017.

cau_hoi: In 1950, Australia released the myxoma virus to kill wild rabbits. After a few years, what did scientists observe about evolution?
C: The virus became less virulent and rabbits evolved resistance
giai_thich: Initially, the virus killed about 99% of infected rabbits. However, virus strains that killed rabbits too quickly had difficulty spreading, as mosquitoes could only transmit the disease from living rabbits. Less virulent strains allowed rabbits to live longer and spread more. At the same time, disease-resistant rabbits survived and reproduced. This is a classic example of co-evolution between a pathogen and its host, studied for decades.

cau_hoi: The blue Spix's macaw, the parrot that inspired the animated film "Rio," was declared extinct in the wild in 2019. What event occurred in 2022?
A: Some captive-bred individuals were released back into the wild in Bahia (Brazil)
B: The species was moved to Africa
D: Thousands of wild individuals were discovered
giai_thich: The last known wild Spix's macaw, a male, disappeared in 2000. Fortunately, there were a few dozen left in breeding facilities, especially in Germany and Qatar. Thanks to breeding programs, the population increased to over 200 individuals. In 2022, about 20 were released back into the caatinga forest near Curaçá, their natural habitat, and the first young were hatched in the wild.

cau_hoi: What does the Hardy-Weinberg principle (1908) state about allele frequencies in a population?
A: Each generation loses half of the alleles
B: Allele frequencies remain constant across generations if there are no mutations, selection, gene flow, drift, and non-random mating
C: Allele frequencies always double each generation
D: Dominant alleles always replace recessive alleles
giai_thich: British mathematician G. H. Hardy and German physician Wilhelm Weinberg independently demonstrated that recessive alleles do not simply disappear because they are recessive. This principle serves as a "null hypothesis" for comparison: if allele frequencies change, we know an evolutionary force is acting. Hardy initially dismissed applied mathematics, but this became his most famous work among biologists.

cau_hoi: What criteria does Ernst Mayr's (1942) concept of the "biological species" use to define species?
B: Organisms living in the same place
D: Populations that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring and are reproductively isolated from other groups
giai_thich: According to Mayr, horses and donkeys are two species because their hybrids, mules, are usually sterile. This definition is difficult to apply to asexual bacteria, fossil organisms, or hybrid species like wolves and coyotes. Therefore, scientists also use other species concepts based on morphology, genetics, or phylogenetic relationships. Mayr lived to be 100 years old and wrote books until the end of his life.

cau_hoi: American geneticist Sewall Wright proposed which famous metaphor in evolution in 1932?
D: "The adaptive landscape" like a hilly terrain, where populations climb to the "peaks" of adaptation
giai_thich: On this map, each point represents a genotype, and the height indicates the level of adaptation. Natural selection helps populations climb to the nearest peak, but they can get "stuck" at lower peaks. Wright suggested that genetic drift in small populations could help populations descend into valleys and then climb to higher peaks. This metaphor is now used in computer science and economics.

cau_hoi: The "molecular clock" idea proposed by Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling in the early 1960s is based on which observation?
A: The number of chromosomes increases with age
B: The number of differences in protein or DNA sequences between two species increases roughly in proportion to the time since they diverged
C: The rings of wood on a tree trunk
giai_thich: They compared hemoglobin proteins from many species and found that the more distantly related two species are in the fossil record, the more differences there are. By "calibrating" with fossils of known ages, the molecular clock allows estimation of divergence times. In 1967, Vincent Sarich and Allan Wilson used this method to argue that humans and chimpanzees diverged only about 5 million years ago, which caused significant controversy at the time.

cau_hoi: The term "Mitochondrial Eve" from the 1987 work of Rebecca Cann, Mark Stoneking, and Allan Wilson refers to whom?
A: A character in a fairy tale
B: The only woman alive at that time
C: The most recent common ancestor through the maternal line of all living people, who lived in Africa about 150,000 – 200,000 years ago
D: The first woman to walk on the Moon
giai_thich: Mitochondrial DNA is only passed down from mother to child. Tracing the mitochondrial DNA of people today converges on one woman. However, she was not the only woman at that time; many others were also our ancestors through different lines, only their mitochondrial lines have broken. Similarly, "Y-chromosomal Adam" is the common ancestor through the paternal line, and the two did not necessarily live at the same time.

cau_hoi: In 2018, scientists published the genome of "Denny", a girl who lived about 90,000 years ago in Denisova Cave (Siberia). What is special about her?
A: She had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father, making her a first-generation hybrid
B: She had DNA from a chimpanzee
C: She was the first modern human
giai_thich: A small bone about 2 cm long was identified as human bone through protein analysis, then the genome was decoded. The results showed that about half of the genome came from Neanderthals and half from Denisovans. The discovery of a direct hybrid among the few ancient bone samples suggests that ancient human groups may have met and interbred quite frequently when living near each other.

cau_hoi: "The Great American Biotic Interchange" occurred about 2.7 – 3 million years ago. When did it happen and what were the results?
A: When America separated from Europe; dinosaurs moved in
B: When humans built the Panama Canal
C: When the ice melted; fish migrated to the mountains
D: When the Isthmus of Panama connected the two Americas; many species from North America moved down to South America and vice versa
giai_thich: From North America, cats, dogs, bears, camels (the ancestors of the dromedary), horses, and elephants moved south. From South America, marsupials like opossums, porcupines, armadillos, giant ground sloths, and even the 2-meter tall "terror bird" moved north. Species from the north were much more successful, and many carnivorous marsupials endemic to South America went extinct. This is why jaguars and alpacas now live in South America.

cau_hoi: The Laotian rock rat (Kha-nyou), described in 2005, is called a "Lazarus taxon" for what reason?
B: It belongs to a rodent family thought to have gone extinct about 11 million years ago, known only from fossils
C: It can die and come back to life
D: It was found in an ancient tomb
giai_thich: Scientists first saw this rat being sold as food in a market in Thakhek (Laos). Initially, it was classified into a new family, but in 2006, paleontologist Mary Dawson pointed out that it belongs to the Diatomyidae family. The name Lazarus comes from a biblical character who was brought back to life. The coelacanth and Wollemi pine are also examples of this phenomenon.

cau_hoi: According to Joseph Connell's "Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis" (1978), when is species diversity in coral reefs or rainforests usually highest?
A: When disturbances like storms and fallen trees occur at a moderate level, neither too few nor too many
C: When there is never any disturbance
D: When disturbances occur continuously every day
giai_thich: Without disturbance, a few of the strongest competing species will take over all the space. If disturbances occur too frequently, only fast-growing, resilient species will survive. At moderate levels, new gaps continuously open up for many species to coexist. This hypothesis explains why a fallen tree in a forest creates opportunities for many young plants to grow.

cau_hoi: What does the "species-area relationship" in ecology indicate?
B: Each km² has exactly one species
C: Larger areas have more species, but the increase slows down according to a power function
D: Area does not affect the number of species
giai_thich: The rule is often written as S = cA^z, where S is the number of species and A is the area. According to a rough estimation rule, reducing the area of a habitat to 10% could lead to the loss of about half of the species in the long term. Scientists use this relationship to estimate the number of species that could go extinct due to deforestation, although this method has its limitations and controversies.

cau_hoi: The Janzen-Connell hypothesis (1970 – 1971) explains how tropical rainforests can have so many coexisting tree species?
A: Mother trees eat their own seeds
B: Seeds and seedlings growing near the mother tree are easily attacked by specialized pests, so trees of the same species struggle to grow densely together
C: Each tree species needs a specific type of soil
D: Birds carry all the seeds away to other places
giai_thich: Daniel Janzen and Joseph Connell independently proposed the idea: natural enemies like insects and pathogenic fungi concentrate around mature trees and attack seedlings of the same species. Therefore, seedlings of a species are more likely to survive when they are far from the mother tree, leaving space for other species. This mechanism prevents one species from dominating, thus maintaining diversity.

cau_hoi: The "Green World" hypothesis of 1960 by Hairston, Smith, and Slobodkin answers which question?
C: Why does Earth remain green and lush: predators control herbivores, so they do not eat all the plants
giai_thich: The short paper by the three American ecologists argues that herbivores are rarely limited by food, but by predators. This idea initiated research on "top-down control" and food webs. Opponents argue that plants also protect themselves with thorns, toxins, and bitterness, so the world is green because most leaves are unpalatable or not nutritious.

cau_hoi: The young ecologist Raymond Lindeman, who died in 1942 at the age of 27, is famous for what work?
D: Studying energy flow through trophic levels in a small lake, laying the foundation for the "10% rule"
giai_thich: Lindeman studied Cedar Bog Lake in Minnesota (USA) and described the ecosystem in terms of energy: how much solar energy is captured by plants, how much is transferred to herbivores, and then to predators. His paper was initially rejected for being "too theoretical" and was only published thanks to the support of Hutchinson, a few months after he passed away. It became one of the classic papers in ecology.

cau_hoi: The British ecologist Charles Elton introduced which concept in his 1927 book "Animal Ecology"?
A: Pyramid of numbers (trophic pyramid) and ecological niche by role in the food chain
giai_thich: Elton noted that in an ecosystem, the number of small prey is usually much greater than that of large predators, forming a pyramid shape. He also wrote the book "The Ecology of Invasion by Animals and Plants" in 1958, laying the foundation for the study of invasive species. Elton conducted many years of research on Spitsbergen Island in the Arctic, where simple food chains are easy to observe.

cau_hoi: What environmental issue was discovered in North America in 1972 by the long-term research project at Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest (New Hampshire, USA)?
giai_thich: Since 1963, Gene Likens, Herbert Bormann, and their colleagues have measured the chemistry of rainwater and streams in small watersheds. They found that the rainwater here was highly acidic, with a pH as low as about 4, due to sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from distant coal-fired power plants carried by the wind. This long-term data contributed to the 1990 amendment of the Clean Air Act in the U.S., which significantly reduced acid rain.

cau_hoi: What did the famous 1973 experiment at Lake 226 in the Experimental Lakes Area (Canada) demonstrate?
C: Phosphorus is the main culprit causing eutrophication and algal blooms
giai_thich: Scientists stretched a plastic sheet to divide the lake into two halves. One half was supplemented with carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus; the other half only received carbon and nitrogen. Just a few months later, the phosphorus-rich half turned green with algae, while the other half remained clear. The aerial photograph became famous and helped countries enact laws to limit phosphorus in detergents.

cau_hoi: How many safe boundaries are included in the concept of "Planetary Boundaries" proposed by Johan Rockström's group in 2009, and how many boundaries had been exceeded by 2023?
giai_thich: The boundaries include climate change, biosphere integrity, land use change, freshwater use, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, ocean acidification, ozone layer, atmospheric aerosol loading, and "novel entities" like plastics and synthetic chemicals. The 2023 assessment showed that 6 out of 9 boundaries have been exceeded. The ozone layer is currently in the safe zone thanks to the Montreal Protocol.

cau_hoi: The Bramble Cay melomys, living on a small coral island in the Torres Strait, was recorded as the first mammal species to go extinct primarily due to what reason?
B: Climate change: rising sea levels and storm surges flooding the island, destroying vegetation
giai_thich: The island is only about 3 meters above sea level and approximately 5 hectares in size. Between 2004 and 2014, the area of vegetation decreased by about 97% due to seawater inundation. A survey in 2014 found no individuals remaining. In 2016, scientists declared the species extinct, and in 2019, the Australian government officially confirmed it.

cau_hoi: In March 2018, the last male northern white rhinoceros named Sudan died in Kenya. What hope remains for this species?
A: Finding a wild herd in the Amazon
D: Using embryos created from the eggs of the two remaining females and frozen sperm, implanting them into a southern white rhinoceros as a surrogate
giai_thich: The two surviving females are Najin and her daughter Fatu at the Ol Pejeta Conservancy, but both are unable to carry a pregnancy. The BioRescue project has harvested their eggs and created over 30 embryos. In 2023-2024, scientists announced the first successful implantation of a southern white rhinoceros embryo into a female rhinoceros, paving the way for implanting northern white rhinoceros embryos.

cau_hoi: What was the first biosphere reserve in Vietnam recognized by UNESCO in 2000?
giai_thich: Can Gio Mangrove Forest (Ho Chi Minh City) was heavily devastated by chemical agents during the war. After 1978, the forest was replanted mainly with mangrove trees, and it has now become the "green lung" of the city with long-tailed monkeys, crocodiles, and birds. The biosphere reserve includes a strictly protected core area, a buffer zone, and a transition area where humans live.

cau_hoi: Which critically endangered primate species endemic to Vietnam has an upturned nose and currently mainly lives in the limestone forests of Tuyen Quang province (including old Ha Giang)?
giai_thich: The Northern snub-nosed monkey (Rhinopithecus avunculus) was once thought to be extinct but was rediscovered in Na Hang (Tuyen Quang) in 1992, and later in Khau Ca (old Ha Giang). The estimated population is only about 200-300 individuals. They have a white face, pink lips, and a distinctive upturned nose. This is one of the 25 most endangered primate species in the world.

cau_hoi: In 1994, what new mammal species did scientists announce in Vu Quang Nature Reserve (Ha Tinh), just two years after the discovery of the saola?
giai_thich: The large muntjac is a small deer species belonging to the genus Muntiacus, with larger antlers than other muntjac species. Later in 1997, a smaller species called the Truong Son muntjac was also announced. The consecutive discoveries of many new large mammal species in the Truong Son range in the 1990s astonished the global scientific community, as it was thought that most large mammals had long been known.

cau_hoi: What is the current status of the kouprey, described in 1937 from a specimen in the Paris zoo and once chosen as the national symbol of Cambodia?
B: No confirmed sightings in the wild since the 1980s, possibly extinct
giai_thich: The kouprey is a large wild cattle species living in the dry forests of Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, and Vietnam. War, hunting, and diseases from livestock have drastically reduced their numbers. Many camera trap surveys have found no traces. Some studies previously suggested that the kouprey was a hybrid between banteng and domestic cattle, but later DNA analysis confirmed it as a distinct species.

cau_hoi: What did the Miller-Urey experiment in 1953 demonstrate about the origin of life?
C: Cells can spontaneously arise from rocks
D: Amino acids can form spontaneously from a simple gas mixture when subjected to electric sparks simulating lightning
giai_thich: Stanley Miller, while a graduate student of Harold Urey, introduced water vapor, methane, ammonia, and hydrogen into a sealed flask and continuously discharged electricity. After a week, the water turned brown and contained many amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. In 2008, re-analysis of samples preserved by Miller using modern machinery found over 20 types of amino acids. However, the primitive Earth's atmosphere was likely different from the mixture used by Miller.

cau_hoi: Bernard Kettlewell's experiment in the 1950s on the peppered moth was criticized. Which later study reinforced his conclusions?
A: A study showing moths can paint themselves
B: An experiment using robots to catch moths
C: Michael Majerus released nearly 4,900 moths in Cambridge (2001 – 2007) and confirmed that birds ate lighter-colored moths more in polluted areas
giai_thich: Kettlewell was criticized for releasing moths during the day and placing them on tree trunks, where moths might not naturally land. Majerus designed a more careful experiment over 7 years and observed birds eating moths. The results were published after his death. In 2016, scientists also discovered a specific mutation in the cortex gene causing dark coloration, which appeared around 1819.

cau_hoi: In 1981, a strange male finch from another island arrived at Daphne Major (Galápagos). What did the Grant couple witness?
A: Its offspring mated with each other, forming a reproductively isolated "Big Bird" lineage after about 2 – 3 generations
B: It flew away the next day
D: It ate all the finches on the island
giai_thich: The male finch belonged to the large ground finch species from Española Island, mating with the native medium ground finch. The offspring had a distinctive song and different beak size, thus only choosing mates within their lineage. Published in 2017 in the journal Science, this is considered a rare example of a new species potentially forming right before scientists' eyes.

cau_hoi: What is the goal of the Kigali Amendment (2016) to the Montreal Protocol?
C: Gradually reduce HFCs, greenhouse gases that are strong but do not harm the ozone layer
giai_thich: When CFCs were banned, companies switched to using HFCs in refrigerators and air conditioners. HFCs do not destroy ozone but can trap heat hundreds to thousands of times more than CO₂. The amendment was adopted in Kigali (Rwanda) and took effect in 2019. Scientists estimate it could help avoid about 0.3 – 0.5°C of warming by 2100.

cau_hoi: What circumstances surrounded the death of the last known po'ouli, a Hawaiian honeycreeper, in 2004?
B: Was swept away by a storm
D: Died in captivity when scientists captured it to find a mate
giai_thich: The po'ouli was only discovered in 1973 on the slopes of the Haleakalā volcano on Maui. By the late 1990s, only 3 individuals remained, living separately. In 2004, conservationists captured a male in hopes of finding a female, but it died of old age after about two months. The other two were never seen again, and the species was declared extinct in 2019.

cau_hoi: Hamilton's rule (1964), rB > C, explains altruistic behavior among relatives. What do the symbols r, B, C mean?
A: r is the coefficient of relatedness, B is the benefit to the helped individual, C is the cost to the helper
B: r is radius, B is height, C is circumference
C: r is rate, B is mass, C is temperature
D: r is number of offspring, B is number of eggs, C is number of nests
giai_thich: According to British biologist W. D. Hamilton, a gene causing an individual to sacrifice for relatives can still spread, as relatives carry many copies of that same gene. The condition is that the benefit multiplied by the degree of relatedness must exceed the cost. For example, ground squirrels alarm call when they see a predator, even though it exposes themselves, and offspring often call more when relatives are nearby.

cau_hoi: Biologist J.B.S. Haldane is reported to have joked that he would be willing to sacrifice his life to save whom, illustrating the idea of kin selection?
giai_thich: Siblings share an average of 50% of their genes inherited from their parents, so two siblings are equivalent to "one self" genetically. Cousins share only about 12.5%, so eight are needed. This joke is thought to have originated in a pub conversation in the 1950s, about 10 years before Hamilton rigorously developed the theory mathematically.

cau_hoi: In bees and ants, males develop from unfertilized eggs. According to Hamilton, what is the coefficient of relatedness between sister worker bees, compared to mother-offspring?
giai_thich: Males are haploid and have only one set of chromosomes, thus passing on identical genes to all daughters. Therefore, full sisters share 75% of their genes, more than the 50% shared between mother and child. Hamilton suggested this explains why worker bees sacrifice reproduction to raise their sisters. However, queens often mate with multiple males, and ants, which are diploid, also have similar social structures, so this is not the only explanation.

cau_hoi: In 1980, Robert Axelrod's computer tournament on the "Prisoner's Dilemma" showed which strategy was the most effective?
D: "Tit for tat": cooperate on the first move, then mimic the opponent's last move
giai_thich: The simplest strategy, sent by mathematician Anatol Rapoport, won both rounds. It is nice (does not cheat first), knows how to retaliate, but also forgives. Axelrod and Hamilton published a paper in 1981 explaining how cooperation can evolve among non-relatives if they meet multiple times, developing Robert Trivers' 1971 idea of "reciprocal altruism."

cau_hoi: What term did Richard Dawkins coin in his book "The Selfish Gene" (1976) to refer to a unit of culture transmitted from person to person?
giai_thich: Dawkins used the Greek word "mimeme" (that which is imitated) and shortened it to resemble "gene." A meme can be a tune, saying, fashion, or way of doing things, spreading and "mutating" like genes. Today, the term is commonly used for humorous images on the internet. The main idea of the book is to view evolution from the perspective of genes: organisms as "survival machines" created by genes.

cau_hoi: According to Amotz Zahavi's "handicap principle" (1975), why do Thomson's gazelles often jump high in place when they see a cheetah?
B: To demonstrate they are healthy and hard to catch, causing the predator to give up
giai_thich: The behavior of jumping high on all fours is called "stotting". According to Zahavi, a reliable signal must be "costly": only truly healthy individuals can afford to waste energy like that. Cheetahs often choose to chase those that do not jump. Similarly, a heavy peacock tail demonstrates that the male is strong enough to carry that burden. Initially, many opposed this, but a mathematical model in 1990 by Alan Grafen supported the idea.

cau_hoi: What did Ronald Fisher propose the "runaway selection" model for in 1930?
A: The preferences of females and traits of males amplify each other over generations, creating extreme traits like the tail of the bird of paradise.
giai_thich: If females prefer long-tailed males, their offspring will carry both the long-tail gene (sons) and the preference for long tails (daughters). The two traits are linked and increase together like a rolling snowball, until the survival cost becomes too high. This may explain why birds of paradise in New Guinea or long-tailed widowbirds have such strange plumage.

cau_hoi: According to Fisher's argument, why is the ratio of males to females born close to 1:1 in most species?
C: Because the environment is always stable
D: If one sex is rarer, individuals of that sex have more reproductive opportunities, so parents producing the rarer sex will benefit, bringing the ratio back to balance.
giai_thich: Assuming males are rare, each male will have many mates, so the genes that cause parents to produce sons will spread until the ratio balances. This is an early example of "frequency-dependent selection." There are interesting exceptions: in parasitic wasps, when brothers mate with sisters in the same host, mothers produce very few males, as Hamilton explained in 1967.

cau_hoi: In North American sage-grouse, dozens of males gather in a clearing, puffing their chests and dancing for females to choose. What is this mating style called?
giai_thich: In a lek, males do not provide females with food or territory, only genes. As a result, a few males in the center of the lek may mate with most females, while many others do not mate at all. This is very strong sexual selection. Peacocks, manakins, birds of paradise, some species of antelope, and even fish also mate in this lek style.

cau_hoi: What does Eric Charnov's "marginal value theorem" (1976) predict about foraging behavior?
B: Animals should leave a foraging patch when the rate of food intake there drops to the average level for the area
C: Animals should stay in one place forever
giai_thich: A bird foraging for worms in a bush will find worms easy to catch at first, then harder. It should move to another bush when the benefits in the current bush fall below the average, taking into account the time to fly. When bushes are far apart, the animal should stay longer. Experiments with corn sparrows and starlings largely support this prediction. This is part of the "optimal foraging theory."

cau_hoi: The Kihansi spray toad in Tanzania, which lived solely on the mist from a waterfall, went extinct in the wild in 2009 for what reason?
B: A hydroelectric dam drastically reduced water flow over the waterfall, combined with a fungal disease
giai_thich: This tiny toad gives live birth instead of laying eggs, living in an area of only about 2 hectares below the Kihansi waterfall. When the hydroelectric dam built in 2000 reduced water flow by about 90%, a misting system was installed, but the population still collapsed. Fortunately, around 500 individuals were taken to zoos in the U.S. in 2000. Since 2012, toads raised at the Bronx and Toledo zoos have been released back into Tanzania.

cau_hoi: According to the 2017 study by Gerardo Ceballos, Paul Ehrlich, and Rodolfo Dirzo, besides species extinction, what is another major concern?
C: The mass decline in population numbers even among common species, which they call "biological annihilation"
D: Too many new species are emerging
giai_thich: They analyzed about 27,600 terrestrial vertebrate species and found that about 32% are declining in numbers and range. Of the 177 mammal species studied in detail, all have lost at least 30% of their range between 1900 and 2015, and over 40% have lost more than 80%. Lions, which once lived throughout Africa, Southern Europe, the Middle East, and India, are now primarily found in scattered regions of Africa.

cau_hoi: "Muller's ratchet," proposed by geneticist Hermann Muller in 1964, describes what problem in asexual populations?
A: Harmful mutations accumulate and cannot be eliminated, like a ratchet that only turns one way
giai_thich: In sexually reproducing organisms, genetic recombination can produce offspring with fewer harmful mutations than their parents. But in asexual organisms, if the "cleanest" individuals are lost randomly, the population cannot recover them. This is one reason why sexual reproduction is common despite its costs. The Y chromosome in humans, which undergoes little recombination, is also thought to be affected by this.

cau_hoi: "Baldwin effect," proposed by psychologist James Mark Baldwin in 1896, describes what?
A: Genetic traits directly acquired as Lamarck suggested
B: The environment does not affect evolution
D: Learned behaviors in life can guide natural selection, later becoming innate traits
giai_thich: For example, if a group of birds learns to eat a new type of seed, selection will favor individuals with beaks or genes that make this easier. Gradually, the suitable trait becomes innate. Unlike Lamarck, there is no direct transmission of learned behavior to offspring; natural selection remains the mechanism. An example in humans is the ability to digest milk in adulthood after dairy farming.

cau_hoi: In 1982, Stephen Jay Gould and Elisabeth Vrba coined the term "exaptation" (pre-adaptation borrowing function). What classic example illustrates it?
C: Feathers likely originally evolved for warmth or display, then were used for flying
giai_thich: A trait evolved for one function may later be "repurposed" for another function. Many dinosaurs had feathers but could not fly, indicating that feathers appeared before the ability to fly. The lungs of ancient fish later became swim bladders in many fish species. The jaw bones of ancient reptiles gradually became the small bones in the middle ear of mammals.

cau_hoi: The 1979 paper by Gould and Lewontin used the image of "spandrel" in the dome of St. Mark's Basilica (Venice) to criticize what?
B: The tendency to explain every trait of an organism as an adaptation due to natural selection
giai_thich: A spandrel is the triangular space that inevitably appears when placing a dome on arch columns, which is then decorated with beautiful paintings. But they were not built "to" hold paintings. Similarly, some traits of organisms may just be byproducts of other changes. For example, the human chin may not have a separate function but is a consequence of jaw development. The paper sparked lively debate for decades.

cau_hoi: "Dollo's Law" (1893) in evolution states what?
B: Species can easily revert to their ancestors
D: A complex structure that has lost its form during evolution is unlikely to reappear exactly as before
giai_thich: Belgian paleontologist Louis Dollo proposed this idea. For example, sea turtles or whales do not grow back gills when returning to the sea but still breathe with lungs. However, there are controversial exceptions: some frog species seem to have regrown lower jaws after more than 200 million years of absence, and some stick insect species appear to have evolved wings again.

cau_hoi: "Cope's Rule" in paleontology describes which trend?
A: Animal lineages tend to increase in body size over evolutionary time
giai_thich: The rule is named after American paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope. A famous example is horses growing from dog-sized to their current size, or long-necked dinosaurs evolving from small species to gigantic ones over 30 meters long. Larger size helps fend off predators, retain heat, and compete for mates. However, larger species are also more prone to extinction when environments change, and there are many exceptions.

cau_hoi: "Haldane's Rule" (1922) states what about hybrids between two species?
B: Hybrids are always healthier than their parents
D: If only one sex of the hybrid is sterile or dies, it is usually the sex with two different sex chromosomes (like XY)
giai_thich: In mammals and flies, males carry XY; in birds and butterflies, females carry ZW. Haldane noted that the "heterogametic" sex often faces issues. For example, when lions are crossed with tigers, male ligers and tigons are often sterile, while females can sometimes reproduce. This rule applies to many animal groups and is one of the most robust rules regarding speciation.

cau_hoi: The Bateson – Dobzhansky – Muller model explains why hybrids between two recently separated species are often sterile or weak in what way?
A: Each population accumulates its own harmless mutations, but when combined in hybrids, the genes from both sides do not "fit" together
B: Hybrids are always abandoned by their parents
giai_thich: Assuming the ancestors had the genotype aabb. One population has mutation A (AAbb), the other has mutation B (aaBB); each mutation is stable within its genetic background. But hybrids carry both A and B, a combination that has never been selected for "testing", which can cause problems. This idea explains how reproductive isolation gradually forms without any disadvantageous intermediate stages.

cau_hoi: In 1973, John Maynard Smith and George Price used the "Hawk-Dove" game to introduce which concept?
giai_thich: In the game, "hawks" always fight, while "doves" only threaten and then flee. If everyone is a dove, a hawk will win big; but if everyone is a hawk, all get severely injured. The result is a stable mix ratio that no new strategy can invade. Evolutionary game theory explains why many animals fight according to "rituals" instead of fighting to the death.

cau_hoi: "The twofold cost of sexual reproduction", proposed by John Maynard Smith in the 1970s, means what?
A: Males eat twice as much as females
B: An asexual population of all females can reproduce twice as fast as a sexual population, because males do not give birth
C: Sexual reproduction consumes twice as much food
D: Each reproduction must have two females
giai_thich: In a sexual population, half of the individuals are males who do not reproduce, and mothers only pass on 50% of their genes to each offspring. If calculated simply, asexual organisms should have the advantage. The continued prevalence of sexual reproduction indicates it has significant benefits, such as creating variation against parasites (the Red Queen hypothesis) or eliminating harmful mutations. This is still referred to as the "queen of all questions" in evolutionary biology.

cau_hoi: Joseph Connell's classic 1961 experiment with two species of barnacles on the rocky coast of Scotland demonstrated what?
A: The two barnacle species are one species
C: The Chthamalus barnacle can live lower down but is pushed up to higher areas by competition from Balanus, where Balanus cannot withstand desiccation
D: Barnacles do not need to attach to rocks
giai_thich: When Connell removed Balanus from the lower rocks, Chthamalus spread down and thrived. This shows the difference between the "fundamental niche" (where a species can live) and the "realized niche" (where a species actually lives in the presence of competitors). This was one of the first field experiments to clearly demonstrate competition in nature.

cau_hoi: In 1969, Daniel Simberloff and E. O. Wilson conducted which bold experiment on small mangrove islands in Florida?
B: Planting pine trees on the islands
D: Covering with tarps and fumigating to exterminate all insects, then monitoring species return
giai_thich: The islands were only about 11 – 25 m wide. After fumigation, insects and spiders gradually returned from the mainland. Within about a year, the number of species on each island had returned close to previous levels, and islands closer to the mainland had more species than those farther away, as predicted by the island biogeography theory. However, the specific species composition was different from before, indicating that while the number of species balanced out, the species themselves were always changing.

cau_hoi: The "Dynamics of Forest Fragments" project initiated by Thomas Lovejoy in 1979 near Manaus (Brazil) studied what?
A: The impact of fragmenting the Amazon rainforest into differently sized patches on species diversity
D: How to chop down forests faster
giai_thich: When farmers cleared the forest, scientists agreed to retain forest patches of 1, 10, and 100 ha for monitoring. The results showed that smaller forest patches lost bird and primate species more quickly, and "edge effects" such as wind, sunlight, and drought could penetrate hundreds of meters into the forest. Lovejoy was also the first to use the term "biodiversity" in its modern sense in 1980.

cau_hoi: Ecologist Aldo Leopold wrote about "land ethics" in which famous book published in 1949?
giai_thich: Leopold argued that humans should see themselves as members of the land community, which includes soil, water, plants, and animals, rather than as its masters. His famous quote: an action is right when it preserves the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community. In his youth, he hunted wolves, but after witnessing the "green fire" fading from a mother wolf's eyes, he changed his perspective on predators.

cau_hoi: John Muir, the American naturalist of Scottish descent, is famous for what role?
C: Advocating for the protection of Yosemite and co-founding the Sierra Club in 1892
giai_thich: Muir walked about 1,600 km from Indiana to Florida. His writings about the beauty of the Sierra Nevada helped Yosemite become a national park in 1890. In 1903, he took President Theodore Roosevelt camping in Yosemite, contributing to persuading Roosevelt to expand the reserves. Muir is known as the "father of the American national parks."

cau_hoi: In 2015, over 200,000 saiga antelopes in Kazakhstan, about two-thirds of the global population, died within a few weeks. What was identified as the cause?
A: The harmless bacterium Pasteurella multocida suddenly caused disease during unusually hot and humid weather
giai_thich: Scientists found blood infection bacteria in most of the dead animals. This bacterium usually resides in the tonsils of saiga. The previous record hot and humid weather likely triggered it. Saiga have a funny large nose that helps filter dust and warm cold air. Fortunately, the population in Kazakhstan has recovered strongly, reaching over 1 million by 2022.

cau_hoi: Hamilton explained in 1967 why fig wasps often produce very few male offspring compared to females. What is that concept?
B: Local mating competition: when brothers mate with sisters in the same fig, the mother needs fewer males
giai_thich: In fig wasps, wingless males emerge first, mate with sisters inside the fig, then bore a hole for the females to escape and die inside. Since males only compete with each other, producing many sons is wasteful for the mother. Hamilton accurately predicted that the sex ratio would skew according to the number of mothers laying in a fig: the more mothers, the higher the ratio of males. This is one of the most successful quantitative predictions in evolutionary biology.

cau_hoi: Japanese geneticist Tomoko Ohta developed the "nearly neutral" theory in 1973. What is the main idea?
A: Large populations evolve more slowly than small populations in all cases
D: Slightly harmful mutations can spread randomly in small populations, while in large populations, selection eliminates them more effectively
giai_thich: Ohta was a student of Motoo Kimura and expanded the neutral theory. The effectiveness of selection depends on both the harmfulness of the mutation and the population size. In small populations, strong drift makes slightly harmful mutations act nearly neutrally. This theory helps explain why the genomes of species with small populations, such as large mammals, often contain more "excess" DNA than bacteria.

cau_hoi: What does Ronald Fisher's "Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection" (1930) state?
A: All species evolve at the same rate
B: The average rate of increase in the fitness of a population equals the genetic variance of fitness
D: The number of species on Earth remains constant
giai_thich: Simply put, the more genetically diverse a population is, the more it affects survival and reproduction, thus providing more "raw material" for natural selection to act upon, leading to faster evolution. Fisher compared it to the second law of thermodynamics. The theorem has been controversial and misunderstood for decades until George Price clarified it in 1972. Fisher is also considered the father of modern statistics.

cau_hoi: Sewall Wright's "Shifting Balance Theory" proposes that evolution occurs most effectively in what type of population?
A: A species divided into many small, semi-isolated populations, with genetic drift and gene flow among them
D: A huge population mating completely randomly
giai_thich: According to Wright, in small populations, drift can take the population "down the valley" on the adaptive landscape and then climb to a new peak. Successful populations will be larger, sending individuals to migrate to other populations and spread beneficial gene combinations. Fisher opposed this, arguing that selection in large populations is sufficient. The debate between the two lasted for decades and remains unresolved.

cau_hoi: "Haldane's Dilemma" (1957) raises what issue about the rate of evolution?
B: Species cannot hybridize with each other
C: Natural selection has a "cost" in terms of the number of individuals that must die, limiting the number of genes that can be replaced in a given time frame
D: Evolution occurs too slowly to observe
giai_thich: Haldane calculated that for a new beneficial allele to replace an old one, many individuals carrying the old allele must die or reproduce less. He estimated that a population of mammals could only replace about one gene every 300 generations. Kimura used this argument in 1968 to assert that most DNA differences between species must be neutral, contributing to the development of the neutral theory of evolution.

cau_hoi: What contribution did George Gaylord Simpson's book "Tempo and Mode in Evolution" (1944) make?
D: Integrating paleontology into the Modern Synthesis, showing that fossils align with population genetics
giai_thich: Before Simpson, many paleontologists believed in a "mysterious force" that directed species to evolve in predetermined directions. Simpson used statistics to analyze the rate of evolution of horses and other groups, demonstrating that they could be explained by selection and genetic variation. He is also famous for his research on South American mammals and was once skeptical of the continental drift theory, a mistake he later admitted.

cau_hoi: The term "Modern Synthesis" originates from the title of a 1942 book by whom?
A: Julian Huxley, the grandson of Thomas Henry Huxley
giai_thich: The book "Evolution: The Modern Synthesis" summarizes the integration of Darwin's natural selection with Mendelian genetics, Fisher's, Haldane's, and Wright's population genetics, along with contributions from Dobzhansky, Mayr, and Simpson. Julian Huxley was also the first Director-General of UNESCO and one of the founders of WWF in 1961. His half-brother, Aldous Huxley, was a famous writer.

cau_hoi: In his book "Wonderful Life" (1989), Stephen Jay Gould used Burgess shale organisms to argue what?
B: If we "rewind the tape of life," the results of evolution could be very different because history depends heavily on chance
C: Humans are the inevitable outcome of evolution
giai_thich: Gould argued that many strange organisms from the Cambrian period went extinct not due to inferiority but because of chance, so the emergence of humans is not inevitable. Paleontologist Simon Conway Morris, who studied those fossils, countered that convergent evolution suggests similar "solutions" will reappear. The debate over "chance vs. inevitability" continues.

cau_hoi: "The Recapitulation Theory" by Ernst Haeckel, summarized by the phrase "the development of the individual repeats the evolutionary history of the species", is now regarded how?
A: As the foundation of modern genetics
D: Considered wrong in its original form: embryos do not pass through the mature stages of their ancestors, although embryos of species share similarities
giai_thich: Haeckel believed that human embryos successively resembled adult fish and then adult reptiles. In reality, the "gill slits" in human embryos are merely folds similar to those in fish embryos, not gills of adult fish. A more accurate idea is from Karl Ernst von Baer (1828): embryos of species are similar in early stages and diverge as they develop. Modern evo-devo studies this issue based on genes.

cau_hoi: What hypothesis did British ornithologist David Lack propose in 1947 about the number of eggs per clutch of birds?
A: The number of eggs depends on feather color
B: Birds lay a random number of eggs
C: The number of eggs is selected to match the number of chicks that parents can raise the most
D: Birds always lay as many eggs as possible
giai_thich: Lack studied great tits in Wytham Woods near Oxford and swifts. If too many eggs are laid, parents cannot provide enough food for all, leading to weak chicks and high mortality. Later experiments adding or removing eggs showed that birds often lay slightly fewer than Lack's "number", as parents need to conserve energy for future breeding seasons. Lack also wrote the classic book "Darwin's Finches" in 1947.

cau_hoi: The paper "In Honor of Saint Rosalia, or Why Are There So Many Animal Species?" (1959) is by which ecologist?
giai_thich: Hutchinson was inspired while observing two species of water beetles in a small pond near the shrine of Saint Rosalia in Palermo (Sicily). He questioned why there are so many species and suggested that closely competing species often differ in size by about 1.3 times, known as the "Hutchinson ratio". The paper inspired a generation of ecologists, including his student MacArthur.

cau_hoi: "The Paradox of Plankton" (1961) proposed by Hutchinson is what?
D: Dozens of plankton species coexist in a homogeneous water environment with few resources, contrary to the principle of competitive exclusion
giai_thich: According to Gause's principle, the number of coexisting species should not exceed the number of limiting resources, such as light, nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon. Yet a drop of lake water can contain dozens of species of algae. Explanations include: the environment continuously changes with seasons and weather, so no species can eliminate others; predators and viruses attack the most common species; and chaotic dynamics among species.

cau_hoi: "The Unified Neutral Theory of Biodiversity" (2001) by Stephen Hubbell has what controversial idea?
A: Many species distribution patterns can be explained by assuming all individuals are equivalent, differing only due to random birth, death, and migration
C: Each species has a completely distinct ecological niche
giai_thich: Hubbell conducted long-term research on a 50-hectare forest plot on Barro Colorado Island (Panama), where every tree with a diameter over 1 cm was marked and measured. His model predicts the ratio of common to rare species quite well. This theory challenges the traditional view that ecological niche differences are key to coexistence, similar to Kimura's neutral theory that challenged genetics.

cau_hoi: According to the "R*" theory by ecologist David Tilman, when many species compete for a limited resource, which species will win?
C: The species that can survive at the lowest resource level (lowest R*)
D: The species that reproduces the slowest
giai_thich: The species with the lowest R* will gradually deplete the resource below the level that other species need, eliminating them. Tilman tested this with diatoms competing for silicon and phosphate. He is also known for long-term experiments at Cedar Creek (Minnesota) since 1994, showing that grasslands with more plant species have higher productivity and stability during droughts.

cau_hoi: "Pleistocene Park" in Siberia, established by scientist Sergey Zimov in 1996, aims to test what?
B: Planting tropical forests in the Arctic
D: Releasing large herbivores like horses, bison, and moose to transform the moss tundra into grasslands and help keep permafrost colder
giai_thich: Zimov believes that during the Ice Age, mammoths and other large herbivores maintained the "mammoth steppe" covered in grass. They trampled snow in winter, helping the cold penetrate deep into the ground, keeping permafrost from melting and releasing carbon. Light-colored grasslands also reflect sunlight better than dark forests. This is a large-scale "rewilding" experiment, but its effectiveness on a global scale is still debated.

cau_hoi: The Oostvaardersplassen nature reserve in the Netherlands, where Heck cattle, Konik horses, and red deer have been released since the 1980s, has become controversial for what reason?
C: There are no predators, populations grow too large, and many die of starvation in harsh winters
giai_thich: The idea was to let large herbivores naturally shape the wetland landscape without human intervention. However, because the area is fenced and lacks wolves, the population increased to thousands. In the winter of 2017-2018, thousands died or were shot to alleviate suffering, causing public outrage. Since then, the area has begun to control the population. This is a lesson about the limits of "rewilding" in the absence of predators.

cau_hoi: Cabo Pulmo National Marine Park (Mexico) is considered a success story of marine conservation for what reason?
A: It has the most oil tankers
B: After about 10 years of fishing bans, fish biomass increased by about 460%, the highest among studied marine reserves
giai_thich: In 1995, the local fishing community decided to stop fishing and advocated for the establishment of a reserve. A survey in 2009 showed that sharks, groupers, and snapper returned in large numbers. The diving tourism industry provided higher income than fishing. This story proves that the ocean can recover quickly when properly protected and with community involvement.

cau_hoi: The Nagoya Protocol (2010, effective in 2014) under the Convention on Biological Diversity regulates what issue?
A: Access to genetic resources and fair sharing of benefits from the use of genetic resources, such as when a company makes medicine from a plant of a country
giai_thich: Previously, many companies in wealthy countries exploited plants, microorganisms, and traditional knowledge of indigenous peoples in developing countries without sharing benefits. The protocol requires prior consent and benefit-sharing agreements. In 2022, countries also agreed to establish a mechanism for sharing benefits from "digital sequence information", i.e., genetic data on computers.

cau_hoi: In 2010, countries set 20 "Aichi Targets" for biodiversity by 2020. How did the United Nations' 2020 report assess the results?
A: No targets were fully achieved globally, only 6 targets were partially met
giai_thich: The Aichi Targets were adopted at a conference in Nagoya, Aichi Prefecture (Japan). One of the closest targets was to protect 17% of land and 10% of marine areas. However, goals such as ending harmful subsidies, reducing deforestation, and preventing species extinction all failed. This failure is why the Kunming-Montreal framework in 2022 set clearer measurable targets.

cau_hoi: What significant outcome resulted from the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment in 1972 in Stockholm?
C: Establishing the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and designating June 5 as World Environment Day
giai_thich: This was the first major international conference to regard the environment as a global issue. UNEP's headquarters are located in Nairobi (Kenya), making it the first major UN agency based in a developing country. The conference took place from June 5 to 16, 1972, hence the opening day was chosen as World Environment Day. Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi famously stated that poverty is the greatest polluter.
